#8886. How to Diagnose and Fix These Common Bike Noises, Including Pedal Clicking

A bike that squeaks, rattles, and clicks is annoying and frustrating. Use these tips to troubleshoot the most common and mysterious bike sounds.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. So first, you’ll need to know how to diagnose it.

The most common noise makers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Below are the most common culprits of pesky bike noises, including bike pedal clicking. Use these suggestions to help you narrow down and silence them. If you lack the proper tools to fix an issue (or fear a fix is above your skill level), seek assistance from your local bike shop or a trusted bicycle mechanic.

That creaky squeaking you hear as you pedal might mean that your bike’s chain needs lube. Cleaning and lubing your chain is usually a good place to start with any weird noise, but if it doesn’t solve the squeak, you may need to do other drivetrain maintenance or replace the chain.

Your chain should also be the first thing you check if you hear a rattling sound while riding. It could mean the loose, excess chain is contacting your frame (this is commonly called “chain slap”). It can also mean your derailleur is out of adjustment and not shifting properly.

A worn chain can also cause noise. Bicycle chains wear out with use as the bushings and rollers in the chain become worn down by grit and grime. This causes slop to develop and the distance between the pin centers to increase. (This is commonly called “chain stretch,” though the metal in the chain hasn’t actually stretched.)

Generally, when a chain “stretches” by 0.5 percent, it is time to change it. If you ride a lot, a chain checker is handy for knowing when it’s time to replace your chain.

Pro Tip: You can also use a ruler to check chain wear. A fresh chain measures 12 inches from pin center to pin center. If it measures more than 12-¹⁄₁₆ inches, change your chain.

If you notice a noise with every pedal stroke, it might be the pedals themselves. To remedy this, remove your pedals, grease the threads, and reinstall them on your bike (remember, both pedals tighten to the front of the bike). When installing, replace the washers (if any) between the pedal and crank arm.

Another source of squeaks might be your shoes’ cleats. Check that your cleats are tight—a loose cleat bolt can cause headaches. While checking the bolts, check for excess wear. Sometimes, the sounds are a sign that the cleats need replacement. An occasional drop or two of wax-based lubricant on two-bolt cleats can help keep the squeaks at bay.

Pro Tip: If your cleats and pedals get squeaky during a ride, a quick squirt of energy drink or something sugary like Gatorade can sometimes quiet them down until you get home and apply lube.

If your bike has internal cable routing, a rattling noise emanating from inside your frame when going over bumps (or knocking when turning) is commonly caused by derailleur housing or hydraulic brake lines. While the sound is rarely cause for concern, it drives riders crazy and can take you out of the zone when training.

Unfortunately, the fix for this issue isn’t usually quick or easy and requires some advanced mechanic skills (especially if dealing with hydraulic brakes). On some bikes—like Trek’s Boone, which has a port on the downtube for this purpose—it could be as simple as adding a zip tie to hold the cables. Other bikes might require the disassembly of the brake hoses and shifter housing (and even the stem and headset on some bikes) to apply sound-damping foam tubing to the lines.

Thankfully, the fix is much easier on bikes with externally routed cables and hoses that have rattling cables. This noise is usually caused when the housing slaps together over bumps on the trail or rough road surfaces. Some pro mechanics heat-shrink the housing together to prevent the sound, but electrical tape can also be used. Another solution is cable clips that keep the housing and hoses from contacting.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM Dub and RaceFace Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

Not long ago, disc brakes were almost only found on high-end bikes and mountain bikes. However, these powerful stoppers are now common on almost all genres of bikes and at all price levels. And disc brakes make some unique sounds that can drive cyclists bonkers.

A chattering sound coming from your rotors might indicate a loose rotor. Check that the rotor bolts or lockring are sufficiently tight. Most disc brakes with 6-bolt rotors use a T25 Torx to tighten. For Centerlock rotors, a cassette lockring tool is used for internal-style lockrings. For external-type lockrings, a rotor/external BB wrench is used.

If your disc brakes are squealing and screeching when you apply the brakes, the brake pads or rotors may be contaminated. This commonly happens from oil residue thrown up from the road when you ride in the rain, contamination from aerosol lubricants, or any one of dozens of other causes.

If the contamination is not too bad, it can often be cleaned off. To do this, remove the wheel and thoroughly wipe down the disc rotor and pads with a clean shop rag or towel and isopropyl alcohol. If you notice significant discoloration of the rotor or grooves in the pads, either or both may need replacement. Your local bike shop can help get you the correct replacement pads and rotors for your brake system.

Pro Tip: If you swap wheelsets on your bike for different rides or races, recenter the disc brake caliper each time you change the wheel. It takes a few extra minutes but helps ensure brake pads wear evenly and reduces rotor rub.

The occasional zing and ting from disc rotors are normal, and these sounds often come and go during a ride as the rotors heat up under hard braking and cool down afterward. If you hear a continuous pinging noise from the rotors, your rotors might need straightening. Head to the below story for more detailed info on diagnosing and fixing common disc brake issues.

A loose headset usually makes a rattling or thunking sound. And a headset that’s too loose can make your bike handle poorly or even damage your frame or fork beyond repair. To tighten a threadless headset system, loosen the bolts on the side of your stem, then tighten the top cap bolt. Tight the bolt enough to pull the fork, headset, stem, and any headset spacers snugly together (but not so tight that the bars can’t turn freely).

After everything is snug and turns smoothly without play in the bearings, retighten the stem bolts. Use a torque wrench to bring the stem to the manufacturer’s recommended spec (this is sometimes noted on the stem in N/m). Because you have the torque wrench out, this is also a good time to check that your stem’s faceplate bolts are sufficiently tight.

If the rattling doesn’t go away after tightening the headset, take your bike to the shop to be safe. Sometimes, the headset might need a shim spacer—but it’s important to check that it’s not a problem with your fork or steerer tube.

Another common source of creaking is your seatpost—particularly if it occurs only while seated. To fix it, remove your seatpost by undoing the quick release (if there is one) or loosening the hex bolt at its base where it enters the frame.

Pro Tip: Before removing your post, measure the seat height (from the center of the crank bolt to the top of the saddle) with a tape measure. Or, mark the position with electrical tape on the seatpost where it meets the seat clamp or frame.

After removing the post, wipe off any grit on the seatpost and inside the seat tube with a rag, and apply a thin layer of grease or fiber grip compound (if you have a carbon frame or are using a carbon post) inside the seat tube. Finally, reinstall the post, tighten the binder bolt to the correct torque, and check if the post still creaks.

If the post still creaks after applying grease and retightening the binder, the noise might be coming from the head of the post or the saddle rails. To check this, undo the hardware that clamps the saddle and the seat from the post. Then, wipe down the hardware and saddle rails with a rag to remove any grit or grime that built up. Finally, reinstall the seat and hardware and tighten them to the manufacturer’s recommended torque.

Chainrings are noise makers when they loosen up and are often overlooked by riders. And if your bike has replaceable rings (with bolts versus riveted together), tightening chainring bolts is an easy fix.

Use the correct side hex or Torx wrench (often 5mm to T30) to the proper torque value. To help prevent the chainring bolts from coming loose again, apply some thread lock compound to the threads.

Pro Tip: Many chainring bolts use a slotted nut on the backside of the ring. If your chainring bolt spins and will not tighten, use a chainring nut tool to hold the nut while tightening the bolt.

If you hear a constant clicking (especially in certain gears) while pedaling, it might mean a shift cable is stretched. (This cable “stretch” is usually the cable housing and ferrules compressing). Cable stretch requires derailleur adjustment for the chain to sit correctly on the gears and not rub the derailleur cage.

First, ensure the derailleur is aligned and the hanger isn’t bent (see below). Then, adjust the cable tension using the barrel adjuster (usually on the rear derailleur on road or gravel bikes and the shifter for mountain bikes). If this doesn’t solve the clicking, you might need to replace your shifter cable and housing.

A bent or misaligned derailleur hanger can cause a constant clicking sound while pedaling. This part (which connects your rear derailleur to the frame) can bend in a crash or incident. They are often replaceable and cheaper to replace than an entire frame.

A bent derailleur hanger might be easy to spot. However, sometimes, a slight bend can cause clicking and poor shifting. (This is especially true for 12-speed drivetrains where even the slightest bend can cause the chain to skip.) If the derailleur hanger isn’t cracked or bent too far to be saved, a hanger alignment tool can be used to straighten it out.

Sometimes, creaking occurs from the derailleur hanger rubbing against the frame where it’s mounted. To remedy this, remove the derailleur hanger, thoroughly clean the frame and hanger, and apply some anti-seize paste to the surfaces that touch.

Pro Tip: Derailleur hangers always seem to break at inopportune moments (like the night before an important race or a holiday when shops are closed). Hangers are relatively low-cost ($25-$50) so, it’s good to have a spare or two in your toolbox. Derailleurhanger.com is a good source for many hangers, especially for older bikes and out-of-business brands.

If you’re purchasing a new bike soon, look for ones using the new Universal Derailleur Hanger standard. Since this hanger is used on many bikes, it’s commonly stocked by many shops. (It also ensures frame compatibility with SRAM’s latest-generation Transmission drivetrains.) Most bikes using UDH are mountain bikes, but it is now popping up on gravel bikes (like the Santa Cruz Stigmata) and road bikes (like the Ritte Esprit).

A noisy thru axle or quick release might need to be tightened. But if tightening it doesn’t quiet the sound, it’s likely one of two problems. A creak or squeak is often a sign of a dry or dirty thru axle or quick release. Remove the thru axle from the frame or fork, clean it, and re-grease it with a thin coat of bike-specific grease. A clicking sound could signify that a thru axle or QR is cracked or broken. This requires immediate replacement.

Pro Tip: If you remove your wheels to get your bike to and from rides, put the thru axles in the frame or fork during transport. This protects your bike from side-load damage and keeps your thru axle from being left behind on your workbench or the trailhead (or getting lost under a car seat).

Far more uncommon than the issues listed above, a cracked or defective frame can be the reason for a persistent, mysterious noise. Frame defects or cracks sometimes aren’t immediately visible and can be hard to diagnose.

Frame damage (from a crash, shipping damage, etc) can also be the culprit. Hairline cracks in carbon frames can be hard to find with the naked eye. When in doubt, bring the bike to an experienced shop for a full inspection. Some companies that repair carbon frames also offer frame inspections. Ruckus Composites in Portland, Oregon, offers ultrasonic inspection to check frames for cracks and damage.

Sometimes, simply thoroughly washing your bike and cleaning and lubing the chain is all it takes to set everything right again. But if you can’t figure out the issue or aren’t sure how to fix it when you do, it’s always a safe bet to take your bike to your local shop or mechanic for service.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8885. The 10 Best Trail Running Shoes for Trails, Gravel, and More

Impeccable traction and responsive rides await. These are the shoes we lace up before hitting the trailhead.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

This year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I plan on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as new shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

For over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

The Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the issues of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, new midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

Stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s issues.

Vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; new foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and says that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she says.

The shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Salomon Pulsar Trail is a win for us for so many reasons, but the entry point of about $140 is hard to beat. It’s built for runners transitioning from roads or tackling milder trails, blending speed with everyday durability.

This shoe rocks a 29mm heel stack and 23mm forefoot (6mm drop), delivering moderate cushion via TPU-based optiFoam². An Energy Blade TPU insert adds responsive pop and stability without bulk, making strides feel snappy yet protected.

The SensiFit upper with Quicklace locks your foot into the shoe—heel to toe—while breathable mesh keeps swamp feet at bay. The All Terrain Contagrip outsole features 4mm lugs for solid grip on dry dirt, gravel, and roots; it sheds mud decently but slips more on wet rocks.

No rock plate keeps weight low at 9.8 ounces, ideal for non-technical runs.

Wear-tester Rebecca Heflin praises the shoe’s comfort, stability, and versatility, wearing it from road to trail.

“The firmness of the sneaker keeps my foot more in place and safe,” she says. “They took a run or two to break in but then were much more flexible. You could ‘feel’ the ground and what you were running on, but still felt comfortable.” This has largely been my experience as well. For a shoe with some heft, it’s nimble and easy to run in.

The Pulsar Trail has a stable ride; it’s plush underfoot and has Salomon’s signature snug fit. Road-to-trail types will love the smooth pavement transitions. It’s perfect for gravel or mixed surfaces from our earlier breakdown.

Shop Men’s on salomon.com | Shop Women’s on Salomon.com

Saucony Peregrine 16 delivers aggressive trail performance with major upgrades, and a less aggressive drop for a closer-to-the-ground feel. It’s our top pick for technical runners hitting rocks, roots, and mud, thanks to the fact that it’s now softer and grippier than ever.

Stack height hits 32mm heel and 28mm forefoot, powered by more Pwrrun foam for smoother cushioning on long hauls. A Pwrrun+ sockliner is made to add another layer of cushioning and, gross enough, smell issues. But I’ve noticed it also helps protect your feet from creepy crawlies and mud incursion. (Creepy crawlies being the most important by a mile.)

The upper has a snug heel and midfoot with a wider forefoot for toe splay, but not too much that it feels unstable or gives you “squishy toes.” They’re using durable, breathable mesh plus enhanced toe and underfoot protection. A Vibram Megagrip outsole with 4mm lugs grips hard on wet rocks, loose dirt, snow, and roots. The traction is significantly improved over prior models despite shallower depth.

A rock guard plate shields from sharp jabs. And contrary to some other plated trail shoes, it doesn’t feel like you’re running on a cement brick. It’s light and protective without compromising foot motion.

Wear-tester Diane Grim says of the Peregrine 16s, “I LOVE this shoe! Right out of the box, amazing! Lightweight, super comfortable, deep responsive vibram lugs.” She added that though the forefoot was stiff, the shoe eventually conformed to her foot after breaking it in. Lastly, she noted the rock plate and cushioning protected her feet from jabs as she ran over sharp rocks.

The Peregrine 16 fits technical trail types perfectly from our breakdown: deep lugs and armor for rocky descents. The shoe is versatile for mixed or singletrack, too.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

I wasn’t sure if I’d like a trail shoe with Adidas’s energy rods. It didn’t feel like a natural pairing, but I’m sold. The impact protection and bit of easy sturdiness they add is genius. The Lightstrike Pro midsole makes the shoe feel fast, peppy, and fun even on unforgiving surfaces.

That’s the thing that keeps surprising me: I can run hard rock trail for hours and my feet just never come up. I train at ultra distances, and that can murder your feet. These just didn’t.

Some of our testers said the fit was narrow. If you’ve got a wide foot, try before you buy. The flip side is the upper mesh wraps really well once it breaks in, so you get that molded, locked-in feel without cranking the laces. Breathability is fine. Not stuffy, not airy either. On a hot day you’ll notice it.

Where I’d hesitate is technical scrambling: Anything steep and hands-on, anything where you’re placing a foot on an edge and trusting it, and the height and softness start working against you—it gets tippy.So: long runnable rocky stuff, absolutely. Chunky scrambles, I’d grab something lower and firmer.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com

Altra Experience Wild 3 is a fave for road-to-trail trekkers, making mixed surfaces like macadam, packed gravel, and light dirt paths seem easy. Its low-drop design and wide toebox allow for natural strides on urban-trail mashups without the clunk of pure trail beasts.

Stack height clocks 32mm with cushioned but snappy Ego P35 foam for responsive cushion that feels efficient, not mushy. An extremely subtle rocker aids smooth transitions from asphalt to gravel chatter.

The engineered mesh upper fits securely yet roomy up front, with durable overlays and gaiter traps to block debris on chip seal or cracked pavement trails. MaxTrac outsole packs 4mm lugs that grip macadam’s rough texture, dry gravel, and hardpack without slipping, shedding light mud pretty decently. No rock plate keeps it nimble, prioritizing speed over heavy armor.

Wear-tester John Mikovits raves about the Experience Wild 3, saying, “I loved the way the shoe slipped onto my foot and laced up. The upper felt plenty roomy like many within the brand but also felt secure in the midfoot and heel.

“The midfoot felt secure which kept me in place when pivoting, turning, and both up/downhills,” he added. “I felt secure for the whole ride and really did not notice any feeling of lack of stability or [the shoe being] too loose.”

Daily training, tempo efforts, or 10 to 20 mile mixed runs thrive here; it’s forgiving for road runners dipping into trails. Though less ideal for steep tech or deep slop, it crushes with efficiency and comfort on crumbly-heavy routes that blend pavement and dirt.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

Lululemon Wildfeel is a truly versatile trail shoe that’s made for runners who live on flowing singletrack and smooth rail trails. It combines plush comfort and reliable grip for those easy, sometimes muddy, sometimes sandy miles where the path can be unpredictable, and staying nimble is key.

The midsole has dual-density supercritical foam with a cushier heel for shock absorption, and a firmer forefoot for responsive toe-off. This setup helps with stability on undulating singletrack and groomed rail trails.

The sock-like Nulu-lined upper with Lycra-nylon hugs your ankle, acting sort of as a gaiter to block debris on dusty, buggy singletrack. The high-abrasion outsole has 4mm multi-directional lugs that bite reliably on dry dirt, roots, and hardpack rail paths, handling light mud and uneven sections without making you feel wibbly-wobbly.

Tester Ryan Werling loves the Wildfeel, saying, “I looked forward to my runs in this shoe and I felt very confident on any surface (declines/inclines). The Wildfeel is less suited for super-technical steeps or deep slop. However, it nails versatile, fun performance on singletrack/rail trail.

Nike’s ACG (All Conditions Gear) line has leveled up lately, and the Zegama Trail is where I’m the most impressed. The Vibram outsole and aggressive, opposed checkmark lugs dig into packed dirt, wet rock, and sloppy singletrack without ever clogging up. The revised last is the real upgrade over the old model: it cups the outer rim of your foot so completely that it almost reads as a stability shoe underfoot. The Mount To Coast H1 absolutely shreds as a gravel specialist, engineered for lightning-fast fire roads and packed paths where loose stones and chatter try to throw you off your game. Its 6mm drop and minimalist build turn rugged gravel into a smooth, efficient run zone that’s ditching the bulk of tech-trail shoes.

Stack height measures 28mm heel, 22mm forefoot, and has a firm, responsive CircleCell foam midsole that delivers sharp ground feel and peppy energy return on washboard gravel. And a wide toebox is a big bonus for folks who love brands like Altra and Topo.

The featherweight mesh upper with minimal overlays breathes easy and fends off dust kicks. Custom sticky rubber outsole rocks 2mm-shallow, tightly patterned lugs that bite small gravel relentlessly while spacing sheds rocks and dirt fast—no clogging on dry, fast-packed surfaces.

The shoe weighs a scant 7.5 ounces for endless miles.

Testers love its razor-sharp handling on gravel—lugs lock in loose stones for zero slip, moderate drop eases calf strain on long efforts, low stack eats vibrations from rutted fire roads, and wide base shrugs off camber without wobble.

“The fit and comfort of the Mount To Coast is superb,” says tester Liz Fones. “The length felt true-to-size, and the width was generally well-balanced, offering plenty of room without feeling sloppy.”

The H1 is a quintessential gravel shoe: light, grippy, and built for speed on packed dirt and crunchy paths.

I am one of those sick, sick puppies who thinks that strapping on a pack and running 100 miles through the woods is a good time, and the On Cloudultra Pros are my new favorite shoe to do that in. The On Cloudultra Pro dominates trail ultramarathons, built for 50K to 100-mile suffer-fests where relentless cushioning and durability outlast crumbling legs on technical singletrack and endless climbs.

Its beastly but comfy upper and upgraded foams turn multiday epics into (slightly) less painful slogs. Unfortunately, you do pay for the privilege as this is by far the priciest shoe on the list.

Stack height soars to 39mm heel, 35mm forefoot (4mm drop) powered by CloudTec Phase midsole pods—hollow chambers that compress for plush landings then rebound explosively for forward drive—paired with Helion HF Hyperfoam that stays springy across 200+ miles of abuse without packing out.

The Swiss-engineered upper fuses a thermo-mapped, one-piece Speedboard chassis for rigidity and energy return, with reinforced Speed-Lacing and gaiter integration blocking debris on rooty, dusty ultras. I was stable through the most miles I’ve run this calendar year, and the foundation feels protective for heavy runners hauling packs. It’s built for comfort and brutality, and I plan on maxing both out.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com

The Norda 055 is what happens when someone asks, “What if a hyper-technical trail shoe had a really good stack?” It’s an actual max-cushion mountain shoe with a 36mm stack in the heel and 30mm stack in the forefoot, so your quads get a soft landing while the rest of you commits to the descent.

The preferred shoe of ultrarunner Rachel Entrekin, the upper is woven from bio-circular Dyneema, a fiber with a strength-to-weight ratio 15 times that of steel. You can’t kill these shoes, and I know this because I’ve done my best to try. Yes, it costs $325. But it’s the long-haul, ultra-distance, “I have a spreadsheet for my aid stations” shoe. Per mile, it’s a bargain, and you can quote me on that when you explain it to whoever manages your budget.

It’s stable, explosive, and rugged. Basically the Linux kernel of footwear, but it actually looks good. (P.S. I only know what that is because my kid just explained that whole thing to me last night.)

Shop Men’s at nordarun.com | Shop Women’s at nordarun.com

Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

Uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

Trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

Drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

Gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

#8882. Asics Just Announced the Gel-Nimbus 29—Here’s Everything We Know, Plus Where to Get the Nimbus 28 on Sale

One of Asics’ best cushioned trainers just got a major update.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nearly three decades old, the Asics Gel-Nimbus certainly deserves its “Legend” status, a moniker applied to the group of Asics trainers that has formed the core of the brand’s lineup for years. The name is old, but this highly cushioned training shoe certainly isn’t stuck in the past: Asics keeps updating it every year. The latest version, the Gel-Nimbus 29, has just been announced, and it’s a thorough revamp that should be a boon for runners who want a soft, well-cushioned platform underfoot. Here’s what you need to know about this update to one of Asics’ most acclaimed shoes.

The Gel-Nimbus 29 represents a fairly significant update, and the most notable changes are in the midsole. Like previous Nimbuses, this shoe uses a combo of FlyteFoam with a layer of Gel under the heel, but the compounds themselves have evolved. The 29th iteration utilizes FlyteFoam Luxe Plus, a new foam that’s even softer than the FlyteFoam Blast Plus material found in the Gel-Nimbus 28. Asics also says the Gel layer is 65 percent softer. The Gel-Nimbus 29 also has a wide sole shape, which gives it a naturally stable, planted feel, and it has slightly increased outsole coverage for better grip and durability.

Asics hasn’t released a full spec sheet on the Gel-Nimbus 29, but the brand states it weighs 9.8 ounces in men’s and 8.4 ounces in women’s. That’s slightly heavier than the 28, which weighed 9.3 ounces in men’s and 8.1 ounces in women’s, but it compares favorably to competing shoes like the New Balance 1080v15 (9.2 ounces in men’s) and the Brooks Glycerin 23 (10.6 ounces).

Overall, you can expect a very well-cushioned ride with this shoe. The Gel-Nimbus 29 makes an excellent choice for long runs, when you need a comfy trainer to support your feet as the mile count grows. The shoe retails for $170 (the same MSRP as the Gel-Nimbus 28). It’s in preorder now, and it’ll officially go on sale on December 1.

And as one model moves in, its predecessor hits the sale rack: The Gel-Nimbus 28 is available at REI, Amazon, Nordstrom, and Asics for $130, a 23 percent discount. While the 28 lacks the updated midsole found on the 29, it’s still a highly capable shoe (it earned a spot in our best-of guide for Asics earlier this year). RW testers loved its lightweight feel and soft-yet-supportive cushioning, a combination of FlyteFoam Blast Plus and PureGel in the heel. It’s a stellar choice for long runs and slower-paced efforts, and one tester called it “a real pleasure to run in.”

So what’s a runner to do? Here’s my vote: Head over to Asics to preorder your Gel-Nimbus 29, and scoop your pair of discounted Gel-Nimbus 28s to tide you over while you wait.

Michael is a freelance writer with years of experience covering gear and the outdoors for Runner's World and other publications; when he's not writing, he's usually biking, hiking, and running in the mountains around Los Angeles, where he lives.

#8880. No Medal, No Aid Stations, No Crowd: What a Solo Ironman Through a National Park Taught Me

He swam 2.4 miles, biked 112 miles, and ran a marathon—all by himself, through one of America’s most spectacular national parks.

Late last year, a friend in Seattle suggested we train for an Ironman 70.3 from opposite coasts. He did the runs, swims, and bike rides along the Pacific Ocean, and I followed suit along the Chesapeake Bay. We weren’t sure whether we’d meet in the middle for an organized event in Nebraska, or save on travel costs with an unofficial “Do-It-Yourself” approach in our backyards.

About halfway through training, he dropped out because of a knee injury. I soldiered on. After 16 weeks of prep, I felt ready, so I set out on my own—no aid stations or medals waiting at the finish line—and accomplished the trek to Annapolis, Maryland, and back in the middle of a snowstorm, with 84 laps in the community pool counting as my 1.2-mile swim.

Later on, I moved to Jackson, Wyoming, where my runs, swims, and bike rides would take place in the shadow of the Tetons. I decided to increase my training workload to try for a full-distance Ironman, also DIY, in Grand Teton National Park. I doubled everything from the 70.3 training block except for the weekend long runs. The schedule as written would have quickly had me running marathons the day after punishing bike rides that took half a day and marked my longest-ever distances in the saddle.

It wasn’t easy. Trail runs and lake swims easily eclipsed the distances I’d done for my high school cross country and swim teams, respectively. And the time was hard to schedule around my 9-to-5. I found a few encouraging partners to swim, ride, and bike with, but I did the majority of the sessions on my own.

The joy of training in pristine wilderness, as spring turned to summer, turned out to be solid motivation. After missing only a handful of workouts over 16 weeks, I felt ready.

I had done another solo half-Ironman to get a feel for the course, my gear, and my fitness level. The week before my target DIY attempt on August 8, I raced a short gravel triathlon with some friends in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, placing second in the first-timers category.

The week of my taper, I relaxed with virtually no workouts. On the day of my attempt, unfortunately, a thick smoke from a West Coast wildfire filled the valley. The swim felt fine, and the bike ride was issue-free, but I could feel my lungs working overtime. By the time I started the run, I couldn’t fathom the marathon ahead of me. Temperatures crested at 80°F, and I was dipping my face and hands in every available stream.

Seven miles in, I started walking and, from there, it was all over. Doing an Ironman without any of the pressure of an organized event means it’s much easier to quit at any point. And the moment I FaceTimed my parents to fill them in, I knew I could just as easily come back and try again the following weekend. No pricey entrance fee or travel to make up. This is my backyard.

So I waited for the smoke to clear, made sure to do a more reasonable taper, and tried again the following weekend, with some of the nerves already shaken out.

Sure, these are luxuries I wouldn’t have had if I’d done a “real” Ironman. But it’s certainly in line with the ethos of these mountains: Sometimes it’s not your summit day. Buoyed by a friend’s words of encouragement (“You have the fitness; you just need a better day”), I packed up the car again and set off for Jenny Lake.

This time, I had my nutrition more dialed: instead of 20-gram protein bars, I packed apple slices and an egg sandwich. The smoke was gone and overcast skies kept temperatures cool. Halfway through the bike ride, a light rain helped chill me even more.

One hundred miles in, disaster struck. My bike’s rear wheel went flat. Rookie road cyclist that I am, I had failed to heed the advice of a more experienced friend to invest in a patch kit. But the trail gods were smiling on me. I pulled right into the Jackson Lake Lodge, where, to my great luck, a pair of bikepackers on their way down the Continental Divide were happy to share some basic supplies.

In 30 minutes, I was back on the way to Jenny Lake, and made it into the parking lot—just as the tire went flat again. I nervously glanced at the odometer: 112.05 miles. Phew!

I felt I owed it to my trail fairy Don to complete the challenge at this point. In a break from official Ironman rules, I allowed myself headphones and music, figuring they were replacing some of the hype of fellow competitors and spectators on a real course.

After 26.2 medium-speed miles, I clicked stop on my watch and collapsed into the cool waters of Jenny Lake as the pink hues of sunset framed the mountains that had been my guide.

“I will forever be a changed man,” I thought to myself. I slept in late the next day, and returned to work on Monday, proud but mostly unchanged. What followed might surprise you.

As the days became shorter and the water colder, a next goal failed to materialize. I fell off my tri-sport routine and started to tick off a few longer hikes instead. I don’t know if I’ll ever do an actual, sanctioned Ironman.

I admire the YouTubers who inspired me to keep up with my training. I understand the appeal of qualifying for the championships in Hawaii. For me, I was simply curious if my body could string together the distances. It was enough that my friend in Seattle called me a beast.

Oddly, I didn’t feel stronger, or more disciplined, or more motivated than when I had started. It was great to have a distraction from work and the chance to push myself in another realm. But, absent others doing the exact same things at the same time, the distances felt arbitrary.

One blessing of living so close to a national park is there are countless adventures and challenges nearby. A few years ago, I tried my hand at the Teton Triathlon. Also known as The Picnic, this unsanctioned endeavor starts with a 20-mile bike ride to Jenny Lake, which you swim across before climbing Grand Teton, the tallest mountain in the range (its summit is 13,775 feet, about 7,000 feet above the Jackson valley), before descending and doing it all in reverse, swimming back across the lake (about 1.2 miles) and biking back to town. It took me 22 hours, and I’d do it again in a heartbeat.

There’s nowhere else in the country you can do anything quite like it. And, to me, the point is to test yourself, rather than beat a field of neoprene-clad athletes. The joy of completing even an unsanctioned Ironman in Grand Teton National Park paled in comparison to the deep satisfaction I felt after completing The Picnic.

A few friends told me it was more impressive to do the Ironman without competitors and fans urging me on. I understand how the public nature of competition helps some people push through hard training days and the race itself. I don’t know that it would have made a difference for me.

When I ran the Chicago Marathon a few years ago, the mandatory fundraising gave that race meaning. I wasn’t bummed that I didn’t qualify for Boston because I’d still hit my dollar goal.

A few weeks after this summer’s Ironman, I accompanied a man running a 50K route in every state in 50 days to raise $1 million for charity. He said that, after a few years of ultramarathons, he wanted to give his time and effort a greater purpose, and doing it for the Make-A-Wish Foundation did that.

That single slow, conversational 50K holds as much meaning for me as all the work I did for my own Ironman. Maybe because it’s a fraction less selfish. Or maybe because it was shared.

That experience, and that man, have stayed with me. I think both of us are chasing something similar in our non-running lives.

#8879. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8878. What the New Moon in Scorpio Means for You

The new Moon is a time of new beginnings. And the new Moon in Scorpio brings intensity, magic, and the opportunity to turn your shadows into light. It is one of the most powerful new Moons of the year for manifestation. And it is one of the most powerful of your life for remembering something you were not taught, which is that you are the creator of your life. Not a passenger in it. Not a person waiting for the right conditions, the right timing, or the right permission. The creator.

The Moon starts its cycle on Sunday, November 8, 2026, at 11:03 pm PST.

On the new Moon, the Sun and Moon meet in the sky in the same zodiac sign. They rise and set together, syncing their energy and their vibration. Because the Moon sits between us and the Sun, no sunlight reaches the side of it that we can see, and the Moon seemingly disappears. On the night of a new Moon, only stars light the sky, and we are left with the darkest point of the lunar cycle.

We tend to think of darkness as negative, but it is neither positive nor negative. Darkness is the void that all life and all energy spring from, and it is the seat of creativity. When we close our eyes or enter a dark space, the imagination opens and we gain access to our inner world. Darkness also calms the nervous system. The mind quiets, and in that quiet intuition gets louder. We stop searching for answers and start receiving them. We can see our blocks and our shadows, and we can also see our dreams and our true desires. Darkness gives us a more expansive view of who we are and what we want.

Each new Moon is an invitation to align with that darkness and travel to the center of yourself. Every month you get a chance to learn something new about your own hopes, fears, and patterns, to hear your intuition more clearly, and to fine-tune the energy you need to manifest your intentions.

The zodiac sign the Sun and Moon are traveling through gives each new Moon its theme. This month they meet in Scorpio, and the theme is transformation. The intuitive guidance you receive tonight point toward the same work, turning your shadows into your strengths.

Scorpio is the alchemist of the zodiac, and alchemy is not a metaphor here. It is a description of what you are actually able to do. An alchemist takes one substance and turns it into another. That is what you do with energy every single day, whether or not you know you are doing it. Every emotion moving through you is raw material. Every feeling you have ever called too much, too dark, or too dangerous is power in an unrefined form. Scorpio hands you the ability to take any energy and make something out of it.

That is why this new Moon is such a potent point of creation. It does not just help you set an intention. It reminds you who is doing the setting.

The new Moon in Scorpio has a particular quality this year. It arrives after weeks of retrograde in Mercury as well as Venus and five days before they each station direct. You are not walking into this new Moon guessing. You have been exploring. You have already reread the journals, replayed the conversations, and finally felt the things you had been avoiding. Whatever you were unsure of a month ago, you are closer to sure about now. That honesty is not a side project. It is the raw material of your creation.

Most of us were handed a story about how life works. Something out there decides. Luck decides, or the economy, or your family, or the person who did not choose you, or the version of yourself you were told you would always be. It is a quiet story and it runs underneath almost everything.

You are an energetic being living in an energetic universe, and everything around you responds to the frequency you hold. Your thoughts, your beliefs, and your emotions are not commentary on your life. They are the instructions. What you carry, you call in. What you believe is possible sets the outer edge of what shows up. This is not wishful thinking. It is how energy works, and it is working right now whether you are directing it or not.

The only real question is whether you are creating on purpose.

That is what this new Moon is intended to remind you. Scorpio takes you underneath your conscious mind, where the actual instructions are stored. Your conscious intentions are only half the transmission. Underneath them sit the beliefs you absorbed before you could evaluate them, the conditioning society handed you about what you are allowed to want, the shadows carrying the messages that you are too much, not enough, or not the kind of person things work out for. Those run quietly, and they are broadcasting too.

You can write the most beautiful intention, yet if some part of you believes you are not allowed to have it, that part will keep creating the life you already have. This is not a flaw inherent in you. This is simply information you did not have access to until now.

The new Moon in Scorpio gives you access. It opens the doorway to your subconscious and lets you see what is normally hidden. When you look at them honestly, you learn exactly where your creation has been blocked. You also feel your true desires, including the ones you have never been comfortable admitting. The new Moon is the night to own them without shame.

Owning your power is not a feeling that arrives one day. It is a decision you make, usually before you feel ready. It means you stop waiting for someone to confirm that you are allowed. It means you stop handing your authorship to your circumstances, your history, or your fear. It means you accept that the life in front of you is one you have participated in creating, which sounds like blame for about ten seconds and then becomes the most freeing sentence you will ever say. Because if you participated in creating this, you can participate in creating something else.

Scorpio does not let you own your power through positive thinking. It makes you earn it. The price of admission is honesty. You have to be willing to face your emotions instead of manage them. You have to confront your shadows instead of outsource them to the people who trigger you. You have to look beneath the layers of conditioning that society placed on you, the rules about who you should be, what a woman is allowed to want, how much success is too much, and what it costs to be seen so you can find the truth of who you actually are underneath all of it.

What you find is a creator. One who has been there the whole time. It is through honest self inquiry that we change our lives. That look at ourselves is not always comfortable. And it is the doorway to everything.

This new Moon in Scorpio carries an unusual amount of support and an unusual amount of heat. Here is what is shaping it.

Mercury is still moving backward in Scorpio, five days from stationing direct. It has already passed through its cazimi, so the the new mental cycle is underway. This is why tonight feels clearer than the rest of the retrograde. The excavating is nearly done. Write what you know now, and understand that some of it might want a final edit after November 13th. That is not a problem. Intentions are living things.

On the West Coast, the new Moon in Scorpio chart places retrograde Mercury opposite the Midheaven by 1°29. The Midheaven is the highest point of a chart, the most public part of a life, and directly across from it sits the most private, the root. Mercury is sitting down there in the dark, and it is pointed straight up.

That is the entire season of Scorpio in one image. The truth that you have been finding in private is being aimed at your public life. Something you have understood quietly is preparing to be said out loud. Angles shift with location and time of day, so this placement is exact for those of us on Pacific Time, yet the message reaches all of us. What you uncover in the roots does not stay in the roots.

The fire is coming. A week after the new Moon in Scorpio, Mars, the traditional ruler of Scorpio, meets Jupiter in Leo, and the Sun squares them both right afterward. Mars is at 22°41 Leo and Jupiter is at 25°15 Leo, and they are closing in on each other, which will be exact on November 15th. This is the aspect that defines the second half of Scorpio season.

Mars is the traditional ruler of Scorpio. It is the planet of courage, drive, heat, and the willingness to go first. Jupiter expands whatever it touches, makes it larger, louder, and more generous. When the ruler of this season meets the planet of expansion in the sign of the heart, the message is direct. It is time to expand by walking through the fire. Not around it. Through it.

Scorpio has spent three weeks showing you the truth underneath your life, and some of that truth is uncomfortable. Mars conjunct Jupiter says the discomfort is not a stop sign. It is the doorway. The conversation you have been avoiding, the work you have been circling, the desire you have been embarrassed by, the boundary you have not set. Whatever you are willing to move toward grows faster than it would at any other point this year, because Jupiter is standing right there making everything bigger.

Fire is the element of courage and Leo is the sign of the heart. Put those together and this is not reckless action. It is heart-led action. Ask yourself tonight what you would do if you were not afraid of being seen doing it, and let that shape at least one of your intentions.

Venus at 23°19 Libra makes a sextile to Mars at 22°41 Leo, with an orb of only 0°38. That makes it the tightest aspect of the entire new Moon in Scorpio chart, which gives it unusual weight.

Venus is still retrograde, meaning it is still reviewing what you love and what you are worth. Mars is fire, forward motion, courage. A sextile is an open door. It is an opportunity that asks you to reach for it rather than handing it over. So the heart, in the middle of its honest review, is being offered courage. The two energies are cooperating.

This is the aspect that lets you act on what you have discovered about love. It softens Mars so its action comes with grace, and it gives Venus boldness so its honesty comes with follow through. If there is something you need to say to a person you love, this aspect is the one supporting you.

Venus also sextiles Jupiter at 25°15 Leo, within 1°56. The same open door, this time to expansion.

Venus retrograde in Libra is asking whether your relationships are balanced and whether you value yourself the way you deserve. Jupiter says whatever you decide about that is going to grow. This is a generous, warm aspect that expands the heart. It supports generosity, forgiveness where forgiveness is true, and a genuine enlargement of what you believe you are allowed to want.

Notice that both of these sextiles involve Venus retrograde. The heart is in review and the universe is handing it two supportive angles at once. That is a strong signal. Whatever you have learned since October 3rd about love, worth, and value, this new Moon wants you to live it.

Through the lens of Scorpio, emotions are simply energy. Scorpio does not teach us to get rid of intense feeling. It teaches us to transmute it. Emotions carry raw potential. They are powerful. And they change our lives once we learn to direct them.

The first step is acceptance. As you work with the new Moon in Scorpio, ask yourself whether you are hiding from any emotion. What is it you do not want to face? Suppressed feelings still affect you. It is better to acknowledge it. When you hold an emotion consciously, it loses its power to run your life from the shadows and becomes fuel you can actually use. Feel your courage as you move through your feelings.

Then ask what the energy could become. Anger accepted often becomes motivation and clarity. Fear becomes surrender and trust anchored in the present moment. Anxiety points you toward the shadow you are running from and can turn into calm or even excitement. Sadness becomes creativity and self-acceptance. Attachment becomes gratitude and the ability to move forward. Grief, given space, can become some of the most creative energy a human being can hold.

Feel the fluidity of your emotions tonight, and notice how easily they shift from one state into another when you stop resisting them. Nothing in you is wasted. Nothing in you is disqualifying. It is all material. And you are the artist.

So write intentions you are actually willing to walk toward. Not the safe version. Not the one that sounds reasonable to the part of you that learned to want less. Write from the truth Scorpio has been uncovering, and write from the knowledge that you are capable of manifesting anything you truly believe is possible for you.

That last part is the work. Not the wanting. The believing. Scorpio is here to help you clear everything standing between you and that belief.

You hold your destiny in your hands. You always have. Tonight the universe is inviting you to stop setting it down.

#8877. Training on Fatigued Legs Builds Durability—as Long as You Do It Right. Experts Explain How.

These expert-backed strategies help you use fatigue to build speed endurance without risking injury.

Most runners know the feeling: dragging yourself out for a jog when your legs feel like lead.

Your calendar says it’s supposed to be an easy day, but your quads seem to have missed the memo. You settle into a shuffle, wondering how a pace that felt effortless last week could demand so much today.

“Running on tired legs means that your body is in a state of recovery following an effort or stimulus,” says Brad Whitley, DPT, a doctor of physical therapy and clinic director at Bespoke Treatments in San Diego. That effort might come from a hard run or strength session, but emotional and work stress can also contribute, he says.

A run in that state isn’t necessarily a bad idea. Practicing on tired legs can help prepare you for the later miles of a race, when you no longer feel fresh. The trick is knowing when pushing through fatigue is useful to performance—and when a rest day will do you more good.

Simply put, running through some fatigue makes you stronger, both physically and psychologically.

“Running on tired legs helps build resilience in the muscular system,” explains Victoria Sekely, DPT, CSCS, a doctor of physical therapy and certified run coach based in New York City. A more resilient muscular system means your muscles can not only recover faster, but also carry you longer and at a quicker clip.

“When your legs are tired, your muscles are undergoing a biophysiological change,” Sekely explains, which includes building stronger muscle fibers. “If you keep going past that fatigue, that will end in a positive adaptation—meaning you can start to run longer without the fatigue setting in.”

Whitley agrees and highlights the mental benefits: “One of the benefits of running on tired legs can be psychological—that is, teaching your central and peripheral nervous systems [the brain, spinal cord, and all nerves that extend to the rest of the body] that you are able to operate with higher levels of fatigue,” says Whitley. “This is helpful for longer races like a half marathon, marathon, ultramarathon, Ironman, and more.”

While it has its benefits, this training tactic requires thoughtful execution to avoid overtraining or injury.

Whatever you do, if you’re running on tired legs, keep the effort easy. “As a rule of thumb, runners shouldn’t complete high-intensity sprints or long threshold sessions when fatigued, as these types of workouts are when muscle strains can happen,” advises Whitley.

Here are a few strategies for how to practice running on tired legs.

“Initially, the best way to introduce training on fatigued legs would be to complete a run in the morning and a whole-body and/or lower-extremity strength session in the afternoon,” says Whitley. “This allows time for some recovery to occur and then would stress a different physiological system in the afternoon.”

It can feel difficult, but your body will become more resilient as the muscle and tendon capacity increases.

The easiest strategy to try running on tired legs is simply to schedule an easy run right after a long training run or speed workout.

“Running on tired legs is mainly for runners who run more than four days a week, and it will naturally happen if you’re following something along the lines of the 80/20 guideline, where 80 percent of your runs are easy and 20 percent are hard,” says Sekely. “On the days that are hard and followed up with an easy day, your legs will most likely feel fatigued. You are certainly at an increased risk of injury on that day, which is why it’s imperative to keep that easy day easy.”

If you’re increasing mileage or prepping for a long-distance race, consider running twice in one day. “Make the morning run a priority, and the p.m. run can be done at an aerobic pace—think zone 1 to 2—to make up for volume needed for the day,” says Whitley.

There’s a fine line between training smart and overtraining. If you’re not fueling properly or skimping on rest, pushing through fatigue is going to backfire, says Sekely.

“It’s important to recognize if you need a rest day—all athletes I work with implement at least one or two rest days every seven to 10 days,” she says. “Every runner benefits from rest days as much as they do easy days.”

Plus, adds Whitley, too much training when you’re feeling tired can mean you’re chronically overtrained—and leave you burned out or with an overuse injury.

So before you head out with heavy legs, check in on a few variables:

Check in with your emotional state before you head out for your run. “If you’re noticing it is incredibly hard to get motivated and you’re having difficulty getting out the door, this might be a sign of chronic fatigue, and you should modify your training schedule,” says Whitley.

Don’t be afraid to take a day or two off, so you feel ready to get back out there.

This is a good guideline to gauge whether you’d benefit more from a run or rest on any given day, says Whitley: If you start your run with moderately fatigued legs and find that you’re not feeling better after moving for 10 minutes, modify the run by making it lower effort (slowing the pace or eliminating hills), or cut it short if you’re seriously struggling.

Heart rate variability measures your individual readiness compared to yourself, and many smartwatches have features to help you easily track yours. If your HRV is way off from your average, Whitley advises opting for a rest day.

When you do call it a day and kick your legs up instead of lacing up to log some miles, remember that you’re not slacking; rest is when the real gains happen.

To get the biggest boost from your time off, Whitley recommends thinking about how you can reduce the root cause of your fatigue—whether that’s doing gentle yoga or getting a massage for sore muscles or meditating to clear a mind that’s been overwhelmed with work stress.

At the end of the day, running on tired legs isn’t about pushing through at all costs—it’s about knowing when to lean into discomfort for growth and when to pull back to avoid burnout.

#8876. The Time of Day You Exercise Could Help Control Blood Sugar

Any physical activity is good for your metabolic health, but research says timing it right may have more benefits for your glucose levels.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Although blood sugar control is essential for those with diabetes, it’s also key for maintaining health overall. Research indicates that blood sugar levels can affect a range of physical functions, including hormone regulation, body composition, digestive processes, and even cognitive health.

That’s why keeping control of blood glucose levels is important, and one way to help might include doing moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise in the evening, according to a study publish in Obesity.

Researchers looked at 186 men and women who were overweight or had obesity and were diagnosed with at least one metabolic impairment, such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Over a 14-day period, researchers tracked their physical activity and glucose levels, along with the time of day for exercise. Morning exercise was defined as before noon, with afternoon exercise between noon and 6:00 p.m, and evening exercise after that.

At the end of the two weeks, those who did more than 50 percent of their exercise in the evening had significantly lower glucose levels compared to those who were sedentary, and better glucose regulation than participants who mainly exercised in the mornings or afternoons.

The effects were especially notable for those who’d struggled with regulating their blood sugar before participating in the study, according to co-author Antonia Clavero Jimeno, Ph.D.(c), researcher in the department of physical education and sports at the University of Granada in Spain.

Although the study participants were specifically chosen based on metabolic factors and sedentary behavior, he told Bicycling that previous evidence has shown that the results might be the same for those without those factors, and who already exercise regularly.

“In fact, the impact of both physical activity volume and timing for glycemic control may be amplified in those with higher activity levels,” he said.

That’s backed up by previous research looking at active people who were assessed for blood sugar changes based on when they exercised. In that study, published in 2022, those who performed moderate-to-vigorous activity in the afternoon had 18 percent lower insulin resistance compared to morning exercisers, and the evening group fared even better, with a 25 percent reduction in insulin resistance.

One factor that was not explored in either study was the role of dietary changes, and this is an area that needs more research, said Clavero Jimeno. Determining whether a strategy like time-restricted eating—also called intermittent fasting—would be helpful or harmful to glucose regulation when paired with evening exercise is a next step, and is already being studied by Clavero Jimeno and his team. (Some research published this year suggests intermittent fasting may have promising effects on blood sugar regulation, at least in those with type 2 diabetes.)

“Dietary intake is, of course, recognized as crucial for glycemic control, and may influence the results overall,” Clavero Jimeno said. “But in the absence of that information, this current study does emphasize that if you want better control of your glucose levels, evening exercise, done at a higher intensity, may be beneficial.”
