## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

In 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the company started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

Since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

Brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

For runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS launched in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

We always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

According to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The new DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

#8872. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8871. Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX Review: Built for Wet, Gritty Miles

The waterproof Gore-Tex upper and grippy lugs handle sloppy gravel—and slick floors during long shifts.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is technically a gravel running shoe, and it excels in that arena. It’s also becoming an absolute cult favorite among nurses, techs, and other healthcare workers who spend 12 hours on slick floors and want something wipeable, grippy, and weather/other substances-tough. Personally, I tested it on the one surface it was born for: wet, gritty, cursed early-morning gravel that always tries to murder me. Tough luck, gravel gods. I’m still alive.

The Gore-Tex of the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is the cold, wet, ugly-conditions sibling in Salomon’s trail running gravel lineup. It’s a boss of a gravel trainer that shares its midsole, outsole, drop, and stack with the standard Grvl running shoe; the difference is that Gore-Tex upper, which trades some airflow and a little weight for weather and moisture blocking power. If you train through damp autumns and slushy winters, like I do, the GTX is 100 percent what you want. If you run mostly in dry, warm conditions, save the $20 and some sweat and take the regular version.

When it comes to the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX, the lugs make the shoe. At 2.5 mm, the lugs aren’t the aggressive, mud-clawing teeth you’ll get on a mountain shoe. They’re short, chevron-shaped, and made of Contagrip rubber that gives you enough hold without digging, and they’re short enough that road-to-trail is totally doable.

I ran them at Shirley Chisholm Park in Brooklyn, which is a landfill-turned-park full of gravel hills. The conditions were damp, slippery, and gloomy. I took them out in the early morning, with loose stone over wet packed base. It’s weather that makes you wonder why you’re there and not at the TJ Maxx across the highway. But, even as a Maxxinista, I settled in fast and happy because the lugs gripped like they were made of sticky tack. My uphills weren’t tripping me up and pulling my toes under my knees, and the downhills didn't turn into a gravel slide. They have just enough give and flex in that rock-protected sole to keep my wobbly body upright, in spite of what gravity would want me to do.

Short lugs also mean less trapped debris and more contact area, which is why the grip carries over to hard, wet surfaces. That’s a big part of the healthcare-worker love: it’s a grippy sole that doesn't feel like a clunky work clog or like you’re rounding in cleats.

The optiFoam² midsole sits in the moderate-cushion zone. It’s soft enough to take the edge off a long shift or a long run, and firm enough that it doesn't feel mushy on uneven stone. It’s not quite a Goldilocks for all situations, but where it works it sings. The 8mm drop is traditional and calf-friendly, so it suits people who are on their feet all day.

It’s not terribly responsive overall, but somehow, in spite of that, it feels fast on gravel, especially on the trickier uphills, where you lose a lot of oomph in most hybrid shoes. It has a nice “settle into your stride” ride feel that gives you a lot of pep for the price. It’s not a racer, but I could see myself racing in them.

The weather in the mornings was, for a period of time, frankly, unholy. My feet stayed dry and comfortable the entire time. My body: not so much. The Gore-Tex membrane handles puddle splash, wet grass, and gravel dust (read: concrete) without seepage, and the upper is easy to wipe down, which is the second reason it’s popular in hospitals and clinics: spills, splashes, and grime aren’t likely to be permanent.

The trade-off is the standard Gore-Tex trade-off: it’s just less dang breathable than a mesh upper, so it runs warmer. Fit-wise, it’s a standard width suitable for most runners—save for those with a really wide midfoot—with a secure, wraparound lockdown.

There’s a quirk to gravel nobody chats about, but I obsess over—the aforementioned concrete situation. The quickLace neo bungee system is great for quick, adjustable fit, but wet gravel dust can dry on the bungee and basically cement it in place. The laces get stuck.

The fix: wet them down a little. A bit of water de-cements the dust and the system moves freely again. Rinse your shoes after dusty runs and you’ll never notice.

Here’s where I must be honest about the limits. This is not the shoe for flat, slabby rock or highly technical trails. The lugs are too shallow to bite into loose, steep, or rooty terrain, and the sole isn’t quite flexible enough to conform around rock features. If your trails look like a scramble, look at a deeper-lugged trail shoe instead.

And it looks good doing it. The number of these I see on chic New Yorkers in my office is wild. But, the important bits, like the abrasion-resistant upper, hold up to gritty, scuffy use, and the reflective details are aces for dark early-morning starts.

Is the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX waterproof? Yes. It uses a Gore-Tex membrane, so it’s waterproof and wind-resistant.

Is it a trail shoe or a road shoe? It’s a hybrid gravel shoe. It’s at home on gravel, fire roads, and mixed paths, but it isn’t designed for technical, rocky trails.

Are Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX shoes good for nurses? Many healthcare workers swear by the third version and are grabbing the fourth for the grip. It’s easy to clean and moisture-resistant.

GTX or standard Grvl? Pick the GTX for wet, cold conditions. Pick the standard version for dry, warm weather and better airflow.

The Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is a stylish, abrasion-resistant, grippy gravel shoe that doubles as a great on-your-feet-all-day option. It’s not a technical trail mistress, or a trail racer, and it isn’t trying to be. For gritty gravel, fire roads, and messy mixed terrain in lousy weather, it’s one of the best new choices around.

#8869. 5 Yoga Poses to Strengthen Your Mid Back (Yes, Your Mid Back)

If you’re seeking ways to strengthen your back, chances are you won’t find a lot of solutions for how to strengthen your mid back. Yoga teacher and certified personal trainer Amber Sayer, who works with desk workers as well as competitive athletes, explains why the missing mid-back component is so essential and how to effectively strengthen it.

When it comes to strength training and your back, almost everyone talks about thinks about avoiding lower back strain or correcting tech neck. But there isn’t much talk about how to strengthen and improve endurance in the muscles of the mid back.

And that’s a shame. This overlooked part of the body not only contributes to your ease of posture and movement during everyday life, it ensures that all of the muscles in your back can work together effectively. Basically, when any part of the back is underutilized, it creates more work for the other parts. Practicing exercises that challenge and build endurance in your mid back supports functional back strength throughout the spine and helps minimize the risk of forcing the muscles in the lower back to overcompensate. Think of your mid-back muscles as one of those things you don’t tend to think about until there’s a problem.

These muscles attach to the thoracic spine and include the middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, and serratus posterior. You’re probably already been practicing yoga poses that strengthen the muscles in the mid back in various ways without realizing it. But when you become more intentional about including these poses each time you’re on your mat, you ensure that you target the various muscles and collaboratively, strengthen your entire back.

Rather than practicing the entire list of yoga poses all at once, incorporate a couple into your mat time whenever you practice, occasionally changing up which ones you explore. Or try a single pose as a one-off whenever you could use a respite from sitting and staring at your screen.

This beginner-friendly pose is your starting point as you’re learning to strengthen the mid-back muscles. Because Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana) props you on your forearms to create the backbend, it can be almost entirely passive for the back muscles. But there are a few subtle actions you can take that engage the mid-back in significant yet non-intense ways.

How to: Lie on your belly with your forehead on the mat and your legs straight behind you, hip distance apart, with the tops of your feet on the mat. Bring your palms and forearms on the mat with your elbows beneath or slightly in front of your shoulders. Actively press down through your forearms to lift your chest off the mat. Draw your shoulder blades down and away from your ears and toward the middle of your back. And the important part for your mid-back is to keep your forearms still but feel as if you’re dragging your elbows toward your hips. Keep that action as you stay here for several breaths.

If the backbend feels too intense, inch your forearms slightly in front of you to lessen how much your chest is lifted from the mat.

This backbend asks you to lift your chest off the mat by pressing your palms to the mat. But when you hover your hands in Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana), you rely exclusively on your mid-back and core muscles to create the shape. The point isn’t how far you lift yourself off the mat. It’s that you create any lift at all.

How to: Start lying on your belly with your palms beneath your shoulders. Start with your palms pressing into the mat and lift your chest. Then press the tops of your feet into the mat and engage your mid-back muscles to lift your chest any amount off the mat. To intensify the workload on your mid-back muscles, lift your palms an inch or two above the mat and continue to hover them. You can also bring your arms straight out from your shoulders like the letter T, and then turn your thumbs toward the ceiling to increase the strengthening potential for the trapezius.

This shape asks you to actively lift your upper and lower body off the mat, which enlists the mid-back muscles as you counteract gravity. It effectively strengthens not only the mid back but the entire back body, including the upper and lower back, glutes, and hamstrings. Locust Pose (Salabhasana) is not easy but it is one of the best back-strengthening yoga poses that exist.

How to: Start lying on your belly with your arms at your sides, palms facing down. Press down through the fronts of the hips and start to lift your upper and lower body off the mat, drawing the shoulder blades toward each other. Lift only as much as you can. Interlace your fingers behind your back and reach your knuckles toward the wall behind you.

This pose is commonly thought of as a quad-strengthening yoga pose, as that’s usually where you feel the burn. But leaning forward in Chair Pose (Utkatasana) without completely collapsing forward and reaching your arms overhead also challenges—and strengthens—the muscles of the mid back. Specifically, the lower trapezius and erector spinae.

How to: From standing, bring your big toes to touch or keep them hip-distance apart. Bend your knees and sit your hips partly back, as if you’re about to sit in a chair. Lean your chest slightly forward and reach your arms alongside your ears. Draw your shoulders away from your ears to strengthen the trapezius and rhomboids.

To intensify the challenge for your your mid back, take any of the following arm variations: • Take your hands farther away from one another to create a V shape with your arms and squeeze your shoulder blades together • Bend your elbows about 90 degrees and create a cactus shape with your arms, being careful not to arch your lower back • Sweep your arms alongside your body, palms facing the mat, drawing your shoulder blades away from your ears

This Warrior pose tends to be less common than Warrior 1 or 2 when it comes to most yoga strength routines, yet it is an unsung hero in terms of strengthening not only the legs but most of the muscles in your body. The trick for targeting the mid-back muscles is to reach your straightened arms in front of you with your torso in Warrior 3 (Virabhadrasana III).

How to: From standing with your hands on your hips or at your chest, shift your weight into one foot and slowly start to lean forward as you lift the other foot and reach it toward the wall behind you. Slowly reach your arms straight ahead, with your arms alongside your ears. Alternatively, you can reach them alongside your body, with your fingertips reaching toward the back wall, in what’s commonly referred to as airplane arms. Imagine actively lifting your straightened arms up toward the ceiling.

#8866. A Frightening Encounter on a Dark Road Nearly Took Night Running From Me. This Year, I’m Taking It Back.

I N THE DARK, the headlights cast a distorted version of my silhouette on the industrial building to my left as the vehicle makes its way past me. I’m running along an otherwise desolate road, not far from my house. The car comes to a halt at the stop sign about 300 feet in front of me—and idles. My legs instinctively slow down, my body reacting before my mind has a chance to catch up. I quickly calculate what to do next. There are no side streets I can turn into—I either have to run past the car or turn around, which would add a few miles to my run that I’m not ready for. Maybe the driver is just checking his phone, I tell myself.

But the broad-shouldered man with a long graying beard at the wheel is waiting for me with the window rolled down, his arm resting in its frame. He starts shouting before I can make sense of the situation: What do I think I am doing, running in the dark? Am I trying to get killed? My body tenses, anticipating the man’s possible next move. He has daughters my age, he continues, and he’d kill them if they did that. Could I at least carry this with me, he roars, throwing a key-chain alarm to my feet, then driving off before I have a chance to react.

I sprint the last half a mile home, propelled by anxious energy. My inability to focus only fuels my confusion; so does the blue egg-shaped alarm in my trembling hand that I don’t have a clear memory of picking up but am holding nevertheless. I try to replay in my head how it got there—and why. I have reflective bands on both my arms and my ankles, so drivers can spot me. I use my phone’s light to illuminate the ground in front of me whenever I need to.

The next day, I don’t run outside in the dark. Too cold, I convince myself when I step on the treadmill I hate so much in my apartment complex gym. Too rattled, is what I am unwilling to admit. Because do I have any right to feel that way when technically nothing happened to me? The stranger, in the end, didn’t hurt me.

Still, something changed on the road in the dark.

With every rhythmic thump the belt makes, I am less determined to keep going. My mind can’t handle the monotony. I start skipping days when I cannot make it out for a daytime run. At some point over the next few weeks, the key to the gym falls behind the shoe rack, and I don’t even notice.

THE LIKELY DIAGNOSIS is seasonal affective disorder. It could also be winter blues, but that one is milder and more temporary. My somber mood and low energy seem constant. For most people, it passes by spring, my therapist says. What helps? For one, exercise! But at that point, my couch’s cushions have resigned to accepting my body’s indentation as their new shape.

By the time spring comes, my fitness is at odds with my enthusiasm for the prolonged daylight, and I end up with shin splints. I spend the rest of the year trying to heal and return to form.

I don’t forget about the gray-bearded man. In fact, I share the story, framing it as a silly encounter. “Would you believe that?” I say with a forced smile.

“That’s not okay,” my friends and coworkers answer with their words as much as their faces.

My feelings start morphing from self-blame into anger. What should have been clear to me from the beginning dawns on me slowly: Vigilance is important, but the solution to a stranger’s concerns about my safety is not to instill more fear in the name of “protection.” Women running at night are not the problem. We’ve long ago dismantled the patriarchal notion that men should be our protectors when, in fact, they often pose the danger.

And so when the clock falls back an hour at the start of November, I’m determined not to fall back into a cycle of seasonal depression and injury.

BY MID-DECEMBER, it’s dark by 4:30 p.m. I wrap my torso in color-changing LED tubes. Today I pick emerald. As I descend the trail that clings to the bank of the Delaware River, the historic cantilever bridge that crosses the water comes into view, itself wrapped in green color-changing lights. I smile for no other reason but that we match.

I run up a semicircle road where, for a moment, the world is reduced to cones of warm yellow glowing from vintage streetlights. My chest lamp illuminates just enough ground in front of me to fit my next two steps. Beyond that, I trust that my feet remember what my eyes cannot see.

The darkness has a way of taming my unruly mind. The stillness mutes my whirling thoughts, a nearly impossible achievement among the hectic noise of daylight. It’s the closest I come to meditating, to understanding what it means to be present. It doesn’t matter where the road leads or how long is left of my run; it’s only here and now. The quiet is mostly disrupted by my own two feet. They take turns striking the ground, but their thuds meet in the echo that reverberates off building walls before getting swallowed up by the endless nightfall blue encircling me.

How did I ever allow this to be taken away from me?

Someone lingers at the end of the sidewalk in front of me, and I instinctively switch to the opposite side, picking up speed.

The person pays me no mind, looking in the direction of a leash they’re holding, the end of which I cannot make out. The black road becomes deserted again, and I slow my pace. What was born out of necessity has grown into my favorite part of the day. I love this. I need this. This is the world I want to live in.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2026 issue of Runner’s World.

#8864. After Training for My First Marathon, I Felt Like My Body Didn’t Look Like the Runner I Thought I’d Become. Experts Helped Me See Otherwise.

Marathon training changed how I saw my body—even when it didn’t change how I looked.

Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.

At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.

Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.

As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.

Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.

So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. But running a marathon is an enormous physical undertaking, and there’s no single body type that proves you’re capable of doing it.

Clinical sport psychologist Hillary Cauthen, PsyD, explains that the concept of “a runner’s body” is “largely a socially constructed ideal influenced by media representation, sport culture, and the tendency to associate certain physical characteristics with athletic success.” She adds that distance running has historically been represented by a lean body type, particularly smaller-framed athletes, which can leave some recreational runners questioning whether they fit the mold.

Comparison is a large part of this problem, too, says Cindra Kamphoff, PhD, mental performance coach and founder of the Mentally Strong Institute. “We see elite runners and start believing that’s what we should look like,” she explains.

Marathon training is practically a master class in comparison, making it hard to avoid. You’re tracking your pace, watching your mileage climb, sharing runs on Strava, and seeing what everyone else is doing. It can feel like your body should be changing right alongside your stats.

There’s also a particularly frustrating point of tension for women, who can feel caught between the cultural expectation to be smaller and the athletic ideal of looking lean and strong. Carinthia Bank, LCSW, a social worker who works with runners on body image, describes this as the “female athlete paradox,” in which women are judged against both ideals.

For example, a woman might recognize that building strength and fueling adequately are essential to marathon training, yet still feel pressure to maintain a smaller frame or worry that eating more to support her mileage will change her body in ways she doesn’t want. These competing expectations can shape how women judge their bodies, even as they get stronger and more capable, Bank explains.

Marathon training can also increase the time we spend thinking about our bodies, particularly when we’re experiencing physical or emotional discomfort, Bank adds. Many runners tend to think they’d feel better if their bodies were different, which can lead to judgment and blame toward the body they have.

That’s the trap I found myself in. While I was training for 26.2 miles, part of me was still measuring my progress against an imaginary finish line where I’d emerge with a completely different-looking body. I would accomplish something I’d never done before, like running my farthest distance, yet I was using my appearance to dictate my progress.

Cauthen offers a simple definition to keep in mind: “A runner’s body is not a specific shape or size. It is a body that runs.”

Here’s the thing about marathon training: Your body adapts to the physical demands of running, but those changes don’t guarantee an aesthetic transformation. You might build muscle, experience weight fluctuations, or notice an increase in appetite as your body works to fuel and recover. “Improved fitness does not always result in weight loss or a smaller body,” Cauthen says.

There’s also a practical reason not to make getting smaller one of your goals in marathon training. Kamphoff encourages runners “to focus on fueling for performance rather than restricting for appearance,” reminding us that “you can’t expect your body to perform at its best if you’re constantly trying to make it take up less space.”

Marathon training requires substantial energy, and restricting food to change your appearance can leave you without enough fuel to support your workouts and recovery.

Plus, fixating on your size can affect more than physical performance. “Focusing on getting smaller can distract and discourage us from actions that are helpful to performance and mental health,” Bank says. When you’re preoccupied with changing your body, you can miss out on learning what helps you perform, enjoying the process, and appreciating everything your body allows you to do.

I had to confront the fact that I’d been treating my appearance as a report card for my training. If I was working hard enough, I assumed I’d eventually see visible proof in the mirror. But I realized I can become a stronger, more capable runner without looking the way I imagined I would.

For me, that meant recognizing that the body I’d been criticizing was the same one carrying me through early morning runs and increasingly long distances. My body wasn’t failing at becoming a runner’s body—I’d been expecting it to meet a standard that had very little to do with what I was asking it to do.

I wish I could say that learning all of this made me instantly love every inch of my body, but that wouldn’t be honest. I’m still working on it, and I still have moments when I catch my reflection and wonder why I don’t look the way I imagined I would after months of training. But I’m trying to shift my focus from what my body looks like to what it’s allowing me to do, with the help of these expert tips.

“One of the most important shifts runners can make is moving from body evaluation to body appreciation,” Cauthen says. Instead of asking whether I look like someone who runs marathons, I’m trying to ask myself what my body has helped me accomplish. And the answer is a lot more impressive than whether or not I have visible abs.

As I got closer to race day, I continued to remind myself that I don’t have to look a certain way to feel proud of what I accomplished. My body carried me through months of training, and that’s worth celebrating all on its own.

I’m also learning to give myself a little more grace when my expectations don’t match reality. Bank reminds runners that “human beings usually get uncomfortable when there’s a difference between what we wanted and what we get,” and encourages compassion rather than self-criticism.

I don’t have to ignore the fact that I expected marathon training to change my appearance, but I also don’t want those expectations to overshadow everything else I’ve gained, including running farther than I ever thought possible, learning how to fuel and maintain energy, and showing up for myself.

Cauthen recommends distinguishing between observing a physical change and assigning a negative meaning to it, which has really stuck with me. “Noticing that your legs have become more muscular, your weight has fluctuated, or your clothing fits differently is an observation,” she explains. “Deciding those changes mean you are too big, not fit enough, or don’t look like a runner is an interpretation.” This helped me realize how quickly I can turn a neutral observation into self-criticism.

Instead of jumping to conclusions, Cauthen says it’s helpful to ask yourself a few questions when those negative thoughts creep in. For example, “is this thought based on evidence or comparison?” and “am I evaluating my body based on appearance or how I feel and function?” These questions challenge the assumptions that we tend to make about our bodies.

Kamphoff encourages runners to develop what she calls an “inner coach” instead of listening to an inner critic. One strategy she recommends is to “capture your wins” by writing down three things you’re proud of after training. The idea is to shift your attention from perceived imperfections to the progress you’ve made.

I’m trying to practice this by celebrating the things that don’t show up in a mirror. For example, I’ve learned how to pace myself and keep going when a run gets uncomfortable. “Your body has been showing up for you mile after mile. Make sure your self-talk is showing up for your body, too,” says Kamphoff.

Ultimately, I’m learning that I don’t need to love how my body looks every single day to respect what it does for me. “Body acceptance does not require loving every part of your appearance every day,” Cauthen says. “Sometimes it starts with respecting your body’s needs and appreciating its efforts, even when your feelings about your appearance are complicated.”

I can have complicated feelings about the way I look and still be proud of the athlete I’ve become. And I can show up at the starting line without meeting some imaginary physical standard first.

That’s the mindset I carried with me to the marathon. I ran 26.2 miles for a cause I believe in, after months of training that challenged me physically and mentally. My body didn’t have to look a certain way to deserve that moment.

After all those early mornings and hours of preparation, I finally crossed the finish line, put the medal around my neck, and walked out of Central Park feeling something I hadn’t quite felt throughout training: pride. Not because my body looked different, but because of everything it had just done. I felt so grateful for my legs that kept moving, my strength that carried me through the tough miles, and a body that got me to the finish line without injury.

No, my body may not have looked like the “marathon body” I once imagined, but it was a marathon body. I didn’t need a mirror selfie to prove what I’d accomplished: I ran all 26.2 miles. Honestly, what could be more impressive than that?

Alyssa is a New York City–based runner and lifestyle writer covering the intersection of fitness, beauty, and everyday routines. Currently training for the NYC Marathon, she brings a firsthand perspective to stories on endurance, recovery, and the mental side of running—alongside the real-life habits that support it. Her work is rooted in what’s practical, personal, and worth incorporating into your own routine.

#8862. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

#8861. The Biomechanics of Speed: How Your Form Can Improve Your Pace

This “speedwork” is way more fun than sprint repeats.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re lacing up your shoes for a 5K or gearing up for a longer endurance race, if you want to get faster, you have to do both longer runs and speedwork sessions to train your aerobic and anaerobic systems. But for the biggest speed gains, you should also look beyond your cardiovascular fitness and work your… posture?

“People often think of running as a lower body sport, but running is everything going on between your ears and everywhere below,” says Anh Bui, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., a former collegiate runner, doctor of physical therapy, and biomechanics specialist in Oakland, California.

While you probably can’t (and shouldn’t) transform your running form into the stride of, say, Olympians on the podium, you can incorporate tweaks to make your mechanics more ideal for you. And that can help you improve performance, get faster, and lower your risk of getting hurt.

“There’s high variability between everyone’s biomechanics based on how you’re structurally and genetically built,” says Bui. “The key is to optimize movement, not force idealism, and to run efficiently to maximize speed and minimize injury risk.”

Read on for more about how each part of your biomechanics, from head to toe, contributes to your speed—plus a handful of moves to add to your routine that’ll help you pick up the pace.

It’s easier to maintain good posture on a short jog versus a long training run when your body starts to drag. But focusing on staying tall and keeping your shoulders from slumping is an important part of efficient running form—not to mention makes it easier to breathe.

Standing up straight as you run with a slight forward lean helps pull you forward, says Ellen Foster, D.P.T., a doctor of physical therapy, movement quality expert, and running coach in Cincinnati. “I like to encourage runners to sort of ‘fall’ forward from the ankles so that their hips are slightly in front of their feet,” she says. “Just make sure you don’t lean forward by bending at the hips or waist, as that would lead to pushing your hips back and losing valuable hip extension.”

Your arms play a surprisingly big role in picking up your pace. Just try pumping your arms harder next time you’re huffing up a hill and see how much it helps. Here’s why: The motion of your arms and legs are linked. “And our arms act as pendulums to help balance our trunk, as forces travel up our body from our legs,” says Foster. “So, when we swing our arms in a more efficient way, our legs often follow their lead.”

While research on just how crucial the arm swing is to running mechanics is limited (most studies focus more on the lower half of the body), and results offer mixed information, most researchers agree that swinging the arms helps with vertical oscillation (or how much we move upward as we stride), side-to-side balance, and minimizing rotation.

“Anecdotally, I find that arm swing drills can be a good starting place when working on increasing cadence, especially if someone is struggling to increase cadence due to poor coordination,” Foster says. Cadence, or the number of steps you take per minute, often changes depending on the speed you’re running, but experts suggest a quicker cadence can limit overstriding and help with forward momentum.

Sprinters tend to drive their knees up aggressively, about 90 degrees from the ground. That’s not sustainable over longer distances, says Bui, who says distance runners should ideally maintain more like 45 degrees of knee drive.

Why does the position of your knees matter? “Picking up your speed without appropriate knee drive will increase likelihood of overstriding, or landing with the foot far in front of your body,” Bui explains. That can slow you down and increases ground reaction forces—or forces exerted by the ground onto the body, Bui says—and ups your chances of injury.

When considering how your feet play into your form and your pace, a lot of it is about those ground reaction forces. If you reduce the time your feet come in contact with the ground, you can potentially lower the force on your body—and lessen your risk of injuries like shin splints, says Foster.

“When we look at vertical ground reaction forces (vGRF) across time, midfoot striking has a lower rate of vGRF with one smooth peak,” Bui explains. By contrast, heel striking has a longer ground contact time, leading to a higher peak force and greater load on the body. This is because your ankle dorsiflexors (when you pull toes toward shins) can’t efficiently absorb the impact of your foot strike, and therefore, your knee joint takes on extra force, she adds.

Try to pick up your cadence and adjust so you’re striking the ground with your foot underneath your body (rather than out too far in front) to help reduce those forces up the leg. Typically, heel striking accompanies overstriding—which can increase risk of injury from the added load—and upping your cadence can help you avoid it.

Keep in mind that your body needs time to adjust to any changes you make in your form. Also, while your body may take on more force with a heel strike, it doesn’t always lead to more injuries or slower speeds. It’s one piece of the biomechanical puzzle. “Heel striking isn’t inherently dangerous by itself,” Foster says.

To improve your biomechanics, working with a run-form coach or physical therapist with advanced training in motor learning or neuromuscular re-education is hugely beneficial, says Foster. “It’s easy to understand the correct biomechanics, but it’s much more challenging to implement them,” she says.

Although working with one of these pros is ideal, a few exercises you can practice on your own can help you get a jumpstart on improving biomechanics.

Here are five biomechanical drills that focus on different aspects of your form. Do them often (for a few minutes as part of your warmup before every run, for example) to make the movements feel like second nature. Then, when you’re working to incorporate tweaks to your form into your run, don’t try to make several changes all at once; try sprinkling them into your runs slowly, thinking about a single form tweak for 30 seconds once per mile.

Just make sure not to jump in too quickly. All tweaks to your body’s biomechanics should be gradual or you risk the chance of injury, says Foster.

Why it works: This super-quick drill emphasizes balance and stability while firing up your posterior chain, which helps develop a more powerful push-off.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Raise right knee to hip height. In a quick, explosive movement, lower right foot to floor and raise left knee high, then lower left knee and raise right knee to hip height again. Do 5 reps. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: Practicing this movement at a quick, consistent pace helps make your arm swing more efficient.

How to do it: Set a metronome app (like Metronome Beats) to a beats per minute that feels in sync with your running cadence; 180 bpm is ideal but dial it back if that feels too quick. Sitting on the edge of a chair or standing with feet hip-width apart, pump arms forward and back to the beat, starting with 10-15 seconds. Do 3-5 sets, resting for about 10-20 second between sets.

Why it works: The plyometric motion of this jump helps prep your tendons to store and release energy quickly. Start by doing the move with both legs, then progress to one leg at a time, recommends Bui.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Keeping legs straight, push off the floor from the ball of feet and swing arms up to jump as high as you can. As soon as you land, jump again. Do 5 reps, jumping as quickly as you can (and minimizing your feet’s contact with the floor). Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: This quick movement increases tendon capacity, trains your body to absorb load as you make contact with the ground, and decreases the time your feet stay in contact with the ground.

How to do it: Stand on the edge of a step or box about a foot tall. With right foot leading, step both feet down to floor. As soon as left foot hits floor, jump up explosively, pushing off floor with both feet. Repeat for 5 steps. Then repeat with left foot leading the step down. Do 2 sets.

Why it works: This move is really just running, with exaggerated motions that mimic ideal sprinting form—and helps develop speed, power, and explosiveness.

How to do it: On a track or long patch of ground, jog forward with as long a stride as possible. As you move, raise the front knee as high as possible while lifting the back foot (keeping leg straight) behind you. Continue for 10 reps total. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training plan.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This plan is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This plan peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.

#8859. 7-Minute Morning Stretch Routine for the Flexibility You (Desperately) Need

Even when you have only seven minutes, you can still complete a practice that releases tension throughout your entire body. The following quick morning stretch routine takes you through an entire sequence of stretch-y yoga poses, focused awareness, and slow breathing.

The following quick yoga routine for your hamstrings, hips, and shoulders can be done in a doable amount of time and will definitely help set the tone for your day and give you that much-needed initial boost of energy. Let’s get started!

You’ll definitely recognize a lot of the poses but there are also some uncommon variations that maximize flexibility. No props are required although you are always welcome to use them.

Kneel on the mat and bring your big toes together, knees apart, and instead of folding straight forward, crawl your hands and fingertips toward the upper left corner of your mat as you fold your chest toward the mat in a version of Child’s Pose. Take 3 big breaths here as you press your hips toward your heels and feel the stretch along your right side body.

Take one more inhale here as you lengthen, and then walk your hands toward the right side of the mat and fold on down. Find lots of length through your left side. One more big inhale through the nose and exhale to let it go. Bring your hands back to center.

Lift onto your hands and knees, palms under your shoulders, knees underneath your hips. Step your right foot in between your hands and keep your knee over your ankle in Low Lunge. As you lift your chest and arms, feel your tailbone lengthen down toward the mat. At the same time, you want to lift out of your lower back so you’re not collapsing there.

Circle your hands to the mat and straighten your right leg. You might need to wiggle your front heel a little farther away from you. Then fold forward over your leg, feeling the stretch in your hamstrings, in Half Splits.

Bend your right knee again. This time, tuck your back toes under, lift your back knee off the mat, and come onto your fingertips into a Runner’s Lunge. Think of pressing your hips down and lifting your heart forward. You might want to rock a little back and forth. Let your hips be heavy, so gravity is doing the work.

Now straighten your front leg any amount and spin your back heel down as if you’re in Pyramid Pose. Keep pressing through both feet. You can shorten your stance if you need in this intense stretch for the hamstrings. See if you can relax your neck and take a breath in through the nose and a long, slow exhalation out the mouth. Stay here for a few more breaths.

Bend into your front knee, plant your hands on the mat, and step back to Downward-Facing Dog. You want your hands to be shoulder-distance apart and your feet hip-distance apart. Bend one knee, straightening the opposite knee and pushing into that heel, and then switch sides.

Inhale as you shift forward into Plank Pose.

Slowly lower all the way down to your belly and take a little backbend here as you lift your chest in Cobra Pose.

Then repeat the previous poses on the other side, including Low Lunge, Half Splits, Runner’s Lunge, Pyramid Pose, and Downward-Facing Dog.

From Down Dog, lean into your left leg, reach your right leg toward the ceiling, bend your right knee, and open up that right hip in Three-Legged Dog. You’re trying to lift your right knee as high as it can possibly go. Then switch sides.

Bring your knees to the mat, sit on your heels, and interlace your fingers behind your lower back. Shrug your shoulders down and away from your ears. Open up as you lift your knuckles away from you.

Stay here or lean forward and lightly bring the crown of your head to the mat and lift your shoulders away from your ears in Rabbit Pose, keeping most of your weight in your knees and feet.

Wherever you are, take a big breath in and then release.

Let’s come to take a seat in any way that is comfortable for you here. Notice how you feel now after just 7 minutes of practice. Stay here for a few long, slow breaths before continuing with your day.

Thank you so much for doing this quick 7-minute morning stretch routine class with me!

#8858. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K

Learn how to tackle the approachable distances with the power of walk breaks.

You’ve completed your Magic Mile time trials, dialed in your pacing, and tracked your progress with your run/walk workouts. Now, it’s time to hit the starting line!

The 5K and 10K make for perfect race distances for beginner and veteran run/walkers alike. Whether you’re shooting to cross your first finish line or earn that big PR, you can train for and race toward your goals with the run/walk method powering every step.

The Runner’s World guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, helps you get to the finish line and cover two of the most popular and approachable distances. Pair our chapter with one of our dedicated training plans to prepare for your first or fastest 5K or 10K yet.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K, we’ll teach you:

Training Principles for Consistent Success

For beginners, a 5K or 10K serves as a great introduction to using the run/walk training strategy for race day. It’s an opportunity to get accustomed to pacing, structure your intervals, and follow a dedicated run/walk training plan. Once you’ve nailed your 5K/10K training block, you may find it easier to bump up to longer distances and chase after new race goals.

But even if you’re not a racing newcomer, a shorter, approachable distance can be an ideal place to start with run/walk. You might even race faster with the run/walk method than you did previously when running the entire distance.

The shorter the distance, the shorter the walk break will likely be, especially if you’re shooting for a PR. Use your data from your Magic Mile test to determine your goal pace for race day.

Some crucial benefits of using run/walk for a 5K/10K include:

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 6-8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 5Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (2 easy runs, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 2 strength train days, 2 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 30-minute run/walk + strength trainingRecommended Experience: For new runners and those who have been running for three months and are ready to do their first race.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 2 strength train days, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 10Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

With one of Runner’s World’s dedicated 5K and 10K run/walk training plans, you can build your endurance and speed for tackling your race. Spanning anywhere from six to eight weeks, our plans include three run/walk days, two to three rest or cross-train days, and even additional easy walk and strength training days, depending on the plan. Whether you’re a beginner looking to dip your toes in run/walk or an experienced run/walker chasing after a personal best, we have a plan tailored to your goals.

Newcomers embarking on their run/walk journey for the first time can also utilize our Couch to 5K training plan. It’s a 10-week plan with two to three days of run/walk, two days of rest, and two days of strength training, aimed at getting you across your first finish line.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska's booking window opens 331 days before departure. For cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and Golden Week (late April through early May), JAL Business Class award space is competitive. Set a calendar reminder and search on JAL.com starting at day 335 — then call Alaska the moment the window opens if you see available seats.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program.
