#8839. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Half Marathon

Run your first or fastest half marathon with the support of walk intervals.

Runners can’t get enough of the half marathon—and for good reason. Not only is it a practical and challenging distance for all levels of runners, but it’s also a race widely offered at running events across the country. Dig through race calendars, and you’ll likely find plenty of half marathons in bucket-list locations and even your own backyard.

And whether you’re looking to run your first or best half marathon, the run/walk method could be the smart, sustainable strategy you need to strongly cross the finish line.

Runner’s World’s program, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, give you the training tools and plans necessary to conquer the 13.1-mile distance with walk intervals. Beginners and experienced run/walkers can find one of several training plans that fit their goals and give them confidence in their physical and mental fitness heading into race day.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Half Marathon, we’ll teach you:

Training Principles for Consistent Success

The half marathon consistently ranks as one of the most popular race distances among runners. According to the 2026 RunningUSA Global Runner Survey, 38 percent of nearly 12,000 surveyed runners said the half was their favorite event—20 percentage points higher than the next most preferred distance (the marathon). The run/walk method can make the distance manageable for all levels of runners and even help you get a new personal record.

“I ran my best half marathon using run/walk during the Savannah Rock ’n’ Roll Half Marathon,” says run/walker Cheryl Munn. “It was really hot. People were dropping like flies. I was able to maintain and be consistent by just keeping up the intervals.”

To find your goal half marathon pace, use your data from your Magic Mile time trial. Multiply your timed mile by 1.2 to get your half marathon race pace. You’ll also use that pace to set your training paces and run/walk intervals you’ll use during your buildup to race day.

Runner’s World has three run/walk training plans to choose from to prepare for your half marathon: a beginner, intermediate, and advanced plan. Over anywhere from six to 16 weeks, you’ll incorporate run/walk workouts, easy walks, long runs, cross-training sessions, and rest days into your training block to build your endurance, speed, and confidence ahead of your half marathon.

Ideal for: Runners who have never completed a half marathon before.

Using this plan, you’ll have two midweek run/walk workouts lasting 30 to 45 minutes each week, along with one easy walk for 20 to 45 minutes, two days with a cross-training option, and at least one rest day. You’ll also have weekend long runs, which start at two miles and work up to 14 miles—longer than the 13.1-mile race distance. Pushing just past the half marathon mark in training will help you build endurance and prepare your body for the

Pro tip: If you’re new to the run/walk method, start your workouts with five to 10 seconds of running, and then walk the rest of the minute. Or, if you’ve been using run/walk for at least three months, you can follow our run/walk ratio suggestion chart to determine your ideal ratio.

Ideal for: Athletes who have been running at least three times a week for three to six months and want to work up from a 5K to a half marathon.

Each week with this plan, you’ll complete two midweek run/walk workouts lasting 30 to 45 minutes, an easy walk, two optional cross-training days, and one rest day. You’ll start with five miles for your first long run and progress to 14 miles by week six. Compared to the beginner plan, the intermediate plan features an increase in mileage.

Ideal for: Runners who have already raced a half marathon before and want to improve their time. You’ll also want to have a solid fitness base before starting the plan, making sure you can complete double-digit miles.

This plan features speedwork once a week, as well as race pace miles one to two times per week based on your Magic Mile time trial. You’ll also have two optional cross-training days and a rest day each week. Your long run begins at five miles and progresses to 14 to 17 miles toward the end of the training block.

A staple speed workout you complete following the advanced plan is 800-meter repeats. You’ll run at 30 seconds per mile faster than your half race pace for 800 meters, followed by 400 meters of walking—which you’ll repeat until you hit your target amount of reps. For example, if your half marathon pace is 12 minutes per mile, you’ll run at 11:30 pace for 800 meters for each rep. For your half marathon pace work, you’ll incorporate race pace miles into both your midweek and long run mileage, allowing you to practice your goal speed and run/walk interval ratios.

Remember all of that patient, consistent work you put in during training? Trust that preparation on race day. It’s tempting to get caught up in the race day atmosphere and complete your first adrenaline-filled miles way too fast. As you begin your race, keep your run/walk ratio and goal pace in mind, and pace yourself strategically in the early miles so you don’t burn out.

The half marathon is such a popular distance that the race course may be flooded with other athletes. As a run/walk athlete, keep in mind that not every runner around you will be taking walk breaks or taking them at the same time as you. Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

#8836. Dragon Pose Is the Essential Recovery Stretch For Tight Hips and Back

The yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

The low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

When shopping for the best under-desk walking pad, keep these factors in mind:

Size and Portability: Ensure the walking pad’s dimensions fit under your desk and in your workspace. Consider weight and whether the machine has wheels for easy storage or movement.

Belt Size: Wider belts provide more stability and comfort, while narrower pads are better for tight spaces. Longer deck lengths work best for those with a longer stride.

Speed Range: Most walking pads offer speeds from 0.5 to 4 mph—enough for gentle walking to brisk paces. Some 2-in-1 pads allow faster speeds when used away from a desk.

Incline Options: A few models feature adjustable inclines for varied intensity, though many are flat for multitasking. If you want more of a workout, look for pads with at least a minor incline capability.

Weight Capacity: Check each machine’s weight limit, especially if you need extra support or want a more robust frame.

Noise Level: Choose a quiet pad for minimal distraction, particularly if you share your space with others or take calls frequently.

Ease of Use: Look for simple controls (often via remote) and clear displays. Consider features like app compatibility, folding capabilities, and maintenance requirements.

Price: Budget models are available for under $200, while high-end or commercial-grade options cost significantly more. Decide which features are worth extra investment for your specific needs.

So, what’s the difference between a treadmill and a walking pad? There are a lot of parallels for sure, and functionally they’re very similar. However, the real difference between a treadmill and a walking pad happens under the hood. Walking pads have smaller, quieter motors that don’t allow you to pick up the pace dramatically, but they keep them quiet enough to use while you work or read. They’re also a lot lower to the ground, and that low step height makes them a great choice for folks who have joint and mobility issues. They’re shorter and narrower than traditional treadmills so that they fit easily under desks. Luckily, they’re also easier to store, and many of them fold into little packages or can be stored on their side. And the point many people love the most? They’re usually a lot cheaper.

Noise: We operated pads during conference calls and regular work to evaluate how quietly each model ran.

Design and Portability: We checked for ease of setup, the ability to move and store the pad, and whether the design fit under multiple desk types.

User Experience: Testers of varying heights and stride lengths used each pad for sessions extending beyond an hour, noting comfort, usability, and any unique features or challenges.

Every product featured here was rigorously tested for durability, performance, and portability in the Runner’s World offices and in the homes of our editors, ensuring our recommendations are both practical and trustworthy. #8831. 11-Minute Stretch and Breathwork Routine to Soothe Your System

Radiance Basden is a certified yoga teacher and passionate advocate for stress reduction, mental resilience, and restorative wellness. Here, she guides readers through a gentle movement and breathwork practice that’s even better when done outside.

It’s a beautiful day to breathe on purpose.

Incorporating grounding practices—including breathing exercises, yoga, and mindful stretching—into your daily routine is one of the the simplest ways to teach your body that it’s okay to relax.

If you have the opportunity to do this sort of breathwork outdoors, the experience can be even more beneficial. When I need to regain my equilibrium, I spend time in nature. After all, outdoor spaces are scientifically proven to soothe your system. Listen to the sounds, notice the world around you, breathe in the fresh air, and embrace the power of simple movements done with intention. You’ll be surprised by how quickly you can come back to yourself.

Begin in a comfortable seat, preferably on the edge of something supportive, whether a chair, couch, bench, even a rock. Place your feet flat on the ground. Both before you start and throughout your practice, check in with yourself and make sure that your shoulders, face, and hands are relaxed.

Rest your hands on your knees—palms facing up to receive energy, facing down for extra grounding. If you feel called to do so, gently close your eyes. Start with 3 deep breaths, slowly inhaling through your nose, slowly exhaling through your mouth.

Now, it’s time to bring in humming breath. Inhale through your nose, and as you exhale, make a humming sound. Continue to hum for the entire length of your exhalation, however long that might be.

Repeat this 5 times or however many you’d like.

Take 3 deep breaths, allowing yourself to sit in stillness while mentally checking in with your body.

Can you still feel the vibrations of your humming?

Make sure your feet are planted about shoulder’s-width distance apart. When you’re ready, begin to move through some hip circles. Circle toward the right, leading with your shoulders and guiding your torso forward, around, and back.

When you’re ready, switch directions and enjoy 8 more circles.

As you move through your hip circles, pay attention to any parts of your body that feel particularly tense or tight and spend some time there. Pause to rock, deepen your stretch, or bring in whatever movement or breath you might need to relax the area.

Next, embody your breath with a seated flow through Cat-Cow. With your inhalation, arch your back and lift your chin toward the sky, bringing your hands to rest on the sides of your hips in a seated variation of Cow Pose.

With your exhalation, round your spine and tuck your chin and bring your hands to rest on the front of your knees in a seated variation of Cat Pose.

Repeat this pattern of movement 10 times, moving with the pace of your own breath.

With your next exhalation, clasp your hands and extend your arms forward in a variation of Seated Forward Bend.

Take 1 full breath here before inhaling your arms up to the sky and exhaling them down at your sides.

Stand up and prepare for a variation of Breath of Joy. Inhale through your nose to throw your arms up overhead, taking a slight backbend in the process.

Exhale through your mouth, making a whooshing sound. Bend forward, bend your knees, and throw your arms back behind you.

Repeat this pattern of movement for 1 full minute.

With you next exhalation, come into Mountain Pose. Stand tall here for 5 cycles of breath through your nose.

Now, for your last bit of breathwork, take 3 more slow breaths, inhaling through your nose and exhaling through your mouth.

#8829. How Runner’s World Training Plans Helped Four Runners Crush the New York City Marathon

Their stories will inspire you to train for your best marathon.

Among the more than 61,000 runners who crossed the finish line of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon were 18 Runner’s World+ members who were part of the Race With Runner’s World+ team. Two were first-time marathoners while 16 others set big goals, such as adding to their World Marathon Major collection and hitting new PRs. No matter their specific ambition, some team members used these Runner’s World+ training plans to power themselves to the Central Park finish line.

Whatever your goal distance and time, you can find a plan by exploring our full training plan collection, including the ones our members used to return to the marathon, earn a sixth star, and run a PR.

🏃‍♀️ Want to run some of the best races in the country with us? Bookmark our Race With Runner’s World+ program page, which gives Runner’s World+ members of all backgrounds and levels a chance at free entry into select races.

Prior to New York, 46-year-old Erin Dewalt ran her last marathon in 2022, a race that she described as a “disaster.” Then, she finished in more than four hours and had an overall rough race day experience.

After a four-year marathon hiatus, Dewalt knew she needed a smart training plan to ensure she would arrive prepared for the NYC Marathon start line. The RW Break 3:45 plan aligned well with her weekly training volume of around four runs per week. For inspiration, she printed the calendar and stuck it to her fridge, checking off completed runs and moving workouts as needed.

The result for Dewalt in the Big Apple? A 3:26:18 marathon performance—breaking the 3:45 barrier by nearly 20 minutes. “I was spot on [with hitting my goal],” Dewalt said after crossing the finish line. “I wanted to enjoy it and have fun but also run around three and a half hours.”

Like Dewalt, Scott Shellabarger printed a Runner’s World training plan, but he used the Break 3:15 plan. In fact, he used it for two races: the NYC Marathon in November and the Flying Pig Marathon in his hometown of Cincinnati, Ohio, in May. “I actually used it for the last marathon I ran, for the Flying Pig, and that’s where I got my PR at,” Shellabarger said. “The training plans are fantastic.”

Not only did the plan help him set a personal best of 3:18:33 at Flying Pig, but it also helped him earn his Six Star Medal in New York and score a 2028 Boston Marathon qualifying time for his age group. Though he didn’t quite break 3:15 with his 3:21:27 performance, it marked his second-fastest marathon to date.

With a hectic schedule as a coach, Courtney Sobanski knew she needed a training plan that could fit into her everyday life. With our 3-Day training plan, Sobanski managed workouts successfully around other responsibilities—and remained injury-free. Our 3-Day plan features three key workouts a week—and any other days of easy running or cross-training you complete count as extra credit.

At the New York City Marathon, Sobanski crossed the finish line in 4:19:09 and told Runner’s World that she showed herself she could still run strong following foot surgery two years ago. “I’m just overcome with emotion that I actually did it and I can [run marathons] again,” Sobanski said following her race.

Ashley Osburn, 41, used the Break 4:30 plan to have every part of her training block mapped out in front of her—intervals, hills, tempo runs, long runs. Osburn said the plan made workouts approachable, and she appreciated the two weekly rest days built into the schedule for better recovery.

Though she didn’t quite reach her sub-4:30 goal in New York due to fueling missteps, Osburn intends to take another shot at the time barrier again in the future. “I will absolutely use [the training plan] again for my next marathon,” she said.

All of our Race With Runner’s World+ members had different goals and training plans pushing them toward the NYC finish line. But they all had a common shared experience of relishing the ecstatic crowds and infectious energy along the course through the five boroughs. “The crowd support all the way through was just amazing,” Dewalt said.

#8828. Trek’s New Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

After riding the $11,499 SLR, I think the $4,200 SL 6 AXS is the smartest buy.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

This Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

If you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the new Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

The version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement

I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

The Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

It hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

And no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

The original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

The new Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek says that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

IsoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also says the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

If you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

According to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

The frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

The internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research showed that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The new frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

The cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

The SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek says both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

The SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

But the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

If you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

Trek says it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

That seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

The fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

The old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the new Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

That’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

What do you think of the new Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

Bicycling members can join me in The Test Ride on Discord to continue this review. The invitation is below.

Find the Trek Gen 5 Domane post in the bike-reviews forum. Tell me what you ride and what you’re deciding between. Your feedback and insights will help me write better reviews.

#8827. A 28-Year-Old Brooklyn Runner Died After Being Stabbed During an Evening Run. Police Are Still Searching for Her Attacker.

Katie Suarez’s death has left runners grieving and residents demanding better safety measures.

(Editor’s note: A 27-year-old man who worked for the city’s public school system was arrested and charged with the murder of Katie Suarez on Saturday, November 7, the New York Times reported.)

On Friday, October 30, Katie Suarez headed out at night along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway Greenway, a waterfront route she'd become quite familiar with from her regular runs around the neighborhood. The 28-year-old was stabbed in the neck that evening and died Monday, November 2, at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, her family confirmed.

The attack came just two days before the New York City Marathon, when the city was already buzzing with runners gearing up for Sunday's race. (Suarez was not registered for the event.) More than 60,000 people would be making their way through the five boroughs that weekend, but Suarez never got to finish her own run. Her death has since shaken the running community, particularly women who know all too well the safety concerns that can come with heading out alone.

Suarez usually met her parents after finishing up at the TD Bank near Caesar's Bay Shopping Center in Bath Beach where she worked, and joined them for the commute home. On the day of the attack, she switched into her running clothes and took off along the waterfront while her parents waited for her to return.

According to The New York Times, her father, Nery Suarez, called just before 8 p.m. to check on where she was. Katie told him she was only about half a mile away and would be back soon, but when more time passed without any sign of her, Nery and his wife, Yasira, became worried and went out looking for her.

Nery eventually found his daughter unconscious just off the running path near Bay 17th Street. She had suffered severe injuries to her neck and was rushed to the hospital, where she remained on life support until her death.

"I'm just left with this pain, and, oh my God, remembering my daughter as she was," Yasira told the New York Daily News on Tuesday. "She just wanted to run.”

As of November 6, police had not identified or arrested a suspect. NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said Monday that investigators were still trying to determine what led to the attack, though they had no reason to believe Suarez was specifically targeted and "right now, it seems that it's random.”

Finding evidence has been especially difficult along the section of the greenway where Suarez was attacked, which is dark and has no reported surveillance cameras. Investigators have searched the surrounding area using everything possible, from drones to police dogs and scuba divers, while also hoping passing motorists might have recorded something useful.

"We are looking for Teslas, we're looking for Uber drivers," Kenny said, explaining that dashcam footage could help police determine whether the attacker crossed the Belt Parkway while escaping.

The lack of lighting has also brought up plenty of concerns from people in the neighborhood who regularly use the path. At a vigil held Wednesday night, neighbors gathered near the waterfront to remember Suarez and discuss what needs to change to make the area safer after dark.

"There's no lights anywhere. It's very dark. A lot of trees, can't see anything," resident Ann Florio-Lopez told ABC7 New York.

Another woman at the vigil said she'd already changed her routine because of the attack, telling the station she “stopped walking at night.”

Runners outside Brooklyn have been speaking up as well, especially with the attack happening so close to marathon weekend. Fast Women shared Suarez's story on Instagram, expressing disappointment that her death hadn't received more attention within the running community. The account also pointed to complaints from locals who had reportedly been asking for better lighting and security along the greenway for years.

For Suarez's younger brother, Christopher, running has taken on a new meaning. He told 1010 WINS that Katie was always looking out for him, often calling to check in whenever he wasn't home at his usual time.

Now Christopher wants to honor her by running “all the miles she wanted to run” and the races she’ll never get the chance to do.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8826. Magnus Ditlev Sets New Iron-Distance World Best With 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida

Magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN)

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

By the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

#8823. ⁠Before You Spend on Gravel Suspension, Try Wider Tubeless Tires for a Simpler, Smoother Ride

Wider tires can add comfort and traction on chunky gravel without the weight of suspension parts.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively new gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate issues and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

After trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

One easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

If they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore new wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

If you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

On my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8822. The 9 Best Running Shoes for Runners With Flat Feet and Low Arches

No, you don’t need more arch support. But here’s what you do need.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 6, 2026: Our Best Overall, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, is 19% off! Our team is currently testing the Adrenaline GTS 26, which is on sale now.

Shopping for running shoes can be especially frustrating if you have flat feet. There are conflicting opinions about what types of shoes best accommodate your foot shape. Some shoe brands add lots of arch support. Other experts say the opposite. What’s a flat-footed runner to do?

Despite the confusion, there are solutions out there, especially with flat feet being more common than you think. Finding shoes that work with your foot type, support good running form, and feel comfortable is paramount—and totally doable.

Not all flat feet are the same, which means there’s no universal solution that will work well for everyone. We’ll go over what it means to have flat feet and some of the potential issues the condition can present for runners. We’ve also highlighted shoe designs that might help alleviate any pain or discomfort you’re experiencing. Finally, we’ve picked the best running shoes for flat feet you can buy right now, including a wide range of options for walking, speedwork, trail running, and more.

Shopping for a daily trainer → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 (Men’s/Women’s)On a budget → New Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s)Searching for some stability → Hoka Arahi 9 (Men’s/Women’s)Adding speedwork to your training → Brooks Ghost Amp (Men’s/Women’s)In need of more cushioned support → Saucony Guide 19 (Men’s/Women’s)Curious about zero-drop → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)Training to race → New Balance SuperComp Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)Racing a marathon → Hoka Rocket X 3 (unisex)Pavement-averse → Hoka Speedgoat 7 (Men’s/Women’s)

Runner’s World Running Reviews Editor Amanda Furrer—who has relatively low arches—researched shoe testing data from our team of approximately 300 wear-testers. Our program includes runners of various experience levels, paces, gaits, and, most important for this guide, arch types. They logged hundreds of miles in these shoes, evaluating comfort, fit, and ride.

Our contributors also gathered intel from industry experts. Caitlin Giddings consulted Kimberly Davis, DC, ART, who is CEO and founder of RunLab in Austin, Texas, and physical therapist Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners. Both Davis and Dicharry have extensive experience assessing and treating runners of all experience levels, gait types, and footwear needs; they were able to provide significant insight on the topic. Michael Charboneau, former RW editor and freelance reviewer for InsideHook, Men’s Journal, and other publications, also offered his expertise in our Q&A section.

Shop the best flat-footed running shoe deals on Amazon

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is as much a runner-fave as its neutral counterpart, the Brooks Ghost 18. This updated version of the Adrenaline GTS features even more cushioning. Brooks heightened the forefoot 3 mm and the heel 1 mm, bringing the offset down from 12 mm to 10 mm. This means more of a balanced feel underfoot. The nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam provides a responsive, plush ride for everyday training and long runs.

Tester Peter Vuong, an overpronator with a flat arch, gave his seal of approval.

“This is a solid, all-around shoe with good flexibility, comfort, and a smooth ride,” he said. “I loved my runs in this shoe. It’s comfortable and laces up nice and snug. The fit is near-perfect. I tested it mostly on the road with a little trail. I would use this shoe for many occasions including a 5K race or nice Sunday 10-miler. It’s nice to have something for multiple uses like that.”

The shoe has the brand’s holistic stability guide rails system. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides of the Adrenaline GTS act as “bumpers” to help align the knee and ankle when form gets erratic from overpronating. Testers said the fit and support were spot-on.

“I’ve run in just about every model of this shoe, many of them predating the guide rails system,” said tester Chris Garges. “This shoe provides the stability that I need as a heel-striking overpronator. I had no issues with the stability even later into a 14-mile training run. Some prior Adrenalines and the Glycerin GTS shoes seem to have a touch too much foot movement, particularly in warm, sweaty weather, which causes blisters or loss of toenails. I did not experience those issues with these shoes.”

Think of the new Ellipse as your run club shoe; New Balance’s newest trainer is meant to make running easier with plenty of pop. The midsole is the brand’s Fresh Foam X, which ensures high energy return on your run as well as plenty of high-cushioned support that absorbs shock. It’s also a generous bed of plush for flat feet.

Testers praised the shoe’s cushioning, even though the ride for some felt slightly bulky. It’s not necessarily a speed shoe, but that didn’t stop some of our testers from going fast on that runner’s high. “It truly feels like I am at an advantage wearing these shoes,” said tester Laura Parks.

“The shoe is SO springy,” she continued. “The best word to describe the cushion is plush. I can feel my foot sinking into the cushion as it molds around me, while simultaneously still feeling the ground. We loved the Arahi 8 so much we bestowed it Gear of the Year. The Arahi 9 preserved all we loved with a few key updates, making the shoe even better. The dual-density compression-molded EVA midsole is retooled so the ride is even softer and more supportive. Think of the new midsole as a plush bed of comfort for your flat feet.

Unchanged is the stability tech. The trainer formerly had the brand’s J-Frame, which was a dense piece of J-shaped foam that wrapped around the heel. The H-Frame, a dense H-shaped piece of foam used in Hoka’s beefier shoes, like the Gaviota, provides a more balanced ride without overcorrecting your gait.

The Arahi 9 kept the previous iteration’s streamlined design. The Hoka team tweaked the fit, making the upper provide more medial support. We like lacing up in this versatile trainer for everyday runs, fartlek workouts, and recovery days.

Like many stability shoes these days, the Guide 19 provides support when you need it. The shoe has Saucony’s CenterPath technology, which uses higher sidewalls and a broader base to help stabilize erratic foot (and ankle and knee) movement. If you thought choosing to run in a low-drop shoe meant a non-supportive barefoot ride (not the ideal for runners with flat feet), then you’ve never run in the Altra Fwd Via 2. Formerly known for making exclusively zero-drop trainers, Altra has released low-drop shoes these past couple of years, welcoming the zero-drop curious into their fold.

Shoes like the Fwd Via 2 have a 4 mm offset, which is merely the height of two stacked nickels. Think of the SuperComp Rebel as the successor to the SuperComp Elite v4, New Balance’s premium racing shoe beloved for its accessible features: a broader base, beefier cushioning for marathoners clocking over five hours, a rocker sole and carbon plate that’s propulsive but not too aggressive. You definitely feel the difference running in sneakers with a carbon plate versus just foam soles. I was more responsive in these New Balance SuperComp Rebels than my regular trainers, New Balance 1080s.”

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

The Rocket X 3 is Hoka-soft with all the super shoe features. The broader base makes this shoe’s fit and ride not as severe as competitors’. Our midfoot didn’t feel squeezed, our toes weren’t crowded, and corner turns didn’t cause our life to flash before our eyes. What you get running in the Rocket X 3 is a stable—but fast—racing experience.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon-fiber plate. Even though its ride is not as aggressive as the brand’s other racing shoe, the Cielo X1 2.0, it still packs a bouncy punch for running half marathons and marathons, and offers plenty of cushioning so your body won’t take a beating hours on the road.

“I love the push-off,” said Erica Bobstein. “They are bouncy and springy and they allow you to propel yourself forward with less effort. They do not have the same speedroll effect as the Saucony Endorphin Pro, but rather have an explosive push-off that requires less energy.”

A combination of plush maximum cushioning and all the tech you need to stay upright on the trail is a winning recipe for flat-footed runners tired of staying on the roads. The Speedgoat gets a reworking with its seventh iteration, resulting in a more secure—albeit, snug for wide feet—fit, and midsole foam that provides comfort for ultra distances.

Toothy lugs provide grip and stability over mixed, technical terrain, while the Meta-Rocker geometry smooths out heel-to-toe transitions. The supercritical EVA foam is tweaked to add more pop on the trail.

Tester Diane Grim, who previously tested the Speedgoat 6, noticed a significant difference in the shoe’s bounce with the 7. She found the ride more forgiving, “which could be great for the long runs, less foot fatigue.”

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Some runners have anatomically flat feet, and other runners have what’s known as “collapsed arches,” which are flat because of a muscle weakness. Although the two types can look very similar, how you approach buying shoes for them varies widely, says Dr. Kimberly Davis of the RunLab, an Austin, Texas-based clinic that assesses running biomechanics and offers physical therapy and training.

Dr. Davis says that when it comes to shopping for a shoe for a flat-footed runner with collapsed arches due to muscle weakness, you can add arch support until the foot gets stronger and can support its own arch. But with an anatomically flat foot, arch support just sends stress up into the knee where it can lead to knee problems.

That’s why it’s important to know what type of flat foot you have before you settle on a shoe—and take into account not just your foot but your entire body, including knees, hips, and range of motion.

Added Arch Support Is Not Always the Answer

Runners with flat feet tend to overpronate, which is when the arches of the foot roll inward after landing. (This isn’t true across the board—there are plenty of flat-footed runners who are biomechanically sound and efficient, and don’t experience any overpronation.)

Up until recently, the running industry steered overpronators toward stability shoes to control this motion. Gradually, all that is starting to change with the realization that stability features don’t do much to correct the natural cycle of the foot, though some runners prefer having them.

Dr. Davis says people with flat feet often have really flexible feet that never get rigid for the push-off. “The footwear industry tries to solve that by putting an arch support in there to give them an arch or create suppination in the foot,” she says. “But that foot is structurally built that way, it’s not something you can solve with a shoe.”

Flat-Footed Runners Can Benefit From a Full-Contact Midsole

Jay Dicharry, author of Anatomy for Runners and director of the REP Lab in Bend, Oregon, agrees arch support can be detrimental because the arch is by nature dynamic, and having extra structure there can stop your foot from moving. Dicharry says flat-footed runners should put more focus on seeking out a shoe with a straight “last,” which is the mold that dictates the shape of the shoe. A straight-lasted shoe has a wider midfoot base and less of a cut-in, a profile that has fallen by the wayside in favor of hourglass-shaped shoes.

Most current shoes don’t provide much of a solid support surface for flat-footed runners, he says. “The problem is all these hourglass shoe shapes look nice on the wall, but when someone with a flat foot puts weight on one, part of their foot is bearing weight on the fabric upper,” he says. “The upper doesn’t work as a midsole for foot support. Feet do well when they’re on an even surface.”

The truth is most running shoes will work for most runners; however, if the shoes you’re using aren’t comfortable immediately or if you’re experiencing any pain while running, you should try a different pair. Get your movement pattern analyzed, whether at a clinic like the RunLab or even a running store that offers gait analysis.

Once you have more information about your feet and movement patterns, you can provide all that information to a running store to find the best shoe for you. Don’t be afraid to take a shoe out for a test run following assessment before purchasing anything.

Here’s a quick way to find out what kind of arches you have: Grab a piece of cardboard and head to the bathroom. Put the cardboard on the floor, wet the bottom of your feet with water in the bathtub or shower, then stand on the cardboard. If you see dry spaces where your arches are, you don’t have flat feet; if you see full footprints showing both soles, then your feet are flat.

As we noted in our explainer, there are multiple kinds of flat feet, and some feet are more flat than others. For a clear, detailed understanding of your foot shape and what kind of foot support you need, you should speak to a podiatrist or running expert.

How can I tell if I have naturally flat feet or collapsed arches?

People with naturally flat feet generally have the condition their entire lives. (Everyone is born with flat feet. Your arches develop in the first few years of life.) Collapsed arches are caused by muscle weakness or an injury. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the most common cause is “inflammation or a tear in the leg tendon (posterior tibial tendon) that supports the arch.”

Both naturally flat feet and collapsed arches can be painful, however, so if you’re experiencing discomfort, it’s best to consult with a doctor to determine which type you have.

My flat feet are causing pain and discomfort. What can I do to alleviate that?

Experts recommend stretching your Achilles, calves, and hamstrings. Stretching those tendons and muscles will help reduce strain on your feet. See our guides to strengthening and stretching the Achilles, calves, and hamstrings for specific exercises.

#8821. This Coach’s Treadmill Strategy Maximizes Fitness, Minimizes Fatigue, and Busts Boredom. Here’s How to Execute It.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

As runners, sometimes we think throwing hills into our runs or pushing the pace a little extra in hard workouts can lead to more gains without consequence. In reality, every time you make your runs a bit faster, longer, or steeper, you have to ease up on something else or you risk burnout, injury, or simply not finishing the session.

Balancing each element of your workout takes some planning. But thankfully, David Siik, founder of Precision Run by Equinox and author of The Ultimate Treadmill Workout, has done the strategizing for you. Siik’s treadmill workout method packs in incline, speed, and distance, without leaving you overly fatigued or struggling to recover the next day. The extra payoff: zero boredom.

Siik’s method combines incline and speed, along with adequate recovery, to gain all the benefits of an interval workout that’s easy to follow. “Once you experience really well-balanced intervals like this, it becomes very easy to know when something feels risky or too stressful on the body,” Siik says.

When you change one element in this workout strategy, you automatically adjust the other elements to manage your fatigue levels and maintain efficiency. For example, when you run intervals at a 1 percent incline, you slow your speed down by 0.2 miles per hour (mph) to prevent overstressing your body.

“It prescribes the right speeds on the right inclines, for the right amount of time so that you are able to maximize your performance while minimizing impact on your body,” Siik says.

The pace for the run portions of this workout should be about 2 mph below your one-minute PR speed. For example, if your one-minute PR speed is 7 mph, run at 5 mph. This pace should feel like a 9 out of 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. It should feel like you could repeat those intervals a few more times without the incline at the end of your workout if you had to.

A shortcut to determining your one-minute PR is to first try running at 5 mph, then go off Siik’s easy guide:

Put that one-minute PR pace setting to use with this workout.

Your outdoor paces don’t always translate directly to the treadmill, Siik explains. You might pace yourself differently because running in place on the treadmill can slightly slow down your times, especially if you’re used to using a GPS watch outside or going off marathon pace, for example, Siik says. That’s why he uses his “one-minute PR” method to help you determine your treadmill pace.

If you go straight to a 9 out of 10 RPE in the very first interval of a 45-minute workout, you might hurt or overexert yourself, Siik explains. It’s okay to start off on the slower end of your effort for the first few intervals, especially as you get more comfortable adjusting to treadmill pace.

Siik recommends starting with a 6 out of 10, then building up from there. This helps you preserve energy for later intervals and leaves you more room to improve.

Even if you’re training for a race, you can still incorporate these workouts into your schedule, in lieu of your weekly interval workout. If you’re going long distance, like a marathon, Siik suggests lowering your run interval pace by 1 mph and bringing your walk breaks up to a pace that’s about 2 mph slower than your run pace.

Siik calls this “cushioning.” “You’re still doing interval training, but the contrast of the hard effort and the recovery become a little less intense,” he adds.

When you have a balance between the amount of speed, incline, and duration you’re running, you don’t overuse your muscles or find yourself struggling to recover. “Increasing workload (incline or speed) too quickly can lead to soreness or risk of injury,” Siik adds. “Small, calculated, progressive increases in incline and/or speed creates a smooth, even increase in work on the body.”

This treadmill workout strategy is designed to make sense to runners who have never run before; it teaches you how to switch back and forth between fast paces and recovery speed, which you might not be used to if you only ever log easy runs or speed up too much on rest intervals.

Most of the time, these types of workouts last between 30 and 45 minutes and include walk breaks, so you’re only running about 60 percent of the time, Siik notes. This makes the workout beginner-friendly.

Each workout follows a pattern, which keeps you more engaged in the intervals and anticipating what’s coming next. “Patternization is the best-kept secret in treadmill running. If you have a pattern that’s really well-structured, your mind knows where the workout is going, and it’s magic,” says Siik.

This also means you’re less distracted, making you more likely to stick with your workout paces and less likely to give up on the session. “When you have a workout that’s really structured and you’re paying attention to the intervals… You do better quality work, then it starts to make more sense to you, and you start making bigger and better goals,” Siik says.

#8820. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

Expert tips for cleat setup, pedal tension, and safe unclipping before your first ride.

When a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”

Not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your new pedals.

I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

In short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

Because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

“Cleat placement is paramount,” says Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”

For those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

“Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” says Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

“Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” says Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

When you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” says Denham.

When I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

“Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”

Then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”

If there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most important piece of the puzzle,” says Quinn.

Once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

Remember how we said switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

“You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” says Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”

The most important thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.
